# Surge

> Static web publishing. One command puts a directory, or a single HTML file, on the web at a *.surge.sh domain or your own, with free custom domains and SSL on every plan.

- Coding agents: start with https://surge.sh/docs/agents (detect the output directory, authenticate with a scoped token, preview, promote on approval, verify, roll back). Skill: `npx skills add https://surge.sh/skills/deploy-to-surge/SKILL.md`.
- Install: `npx surge`, or `npm install -g surge` (Node 18 or newer).
- Publish: `surge <path> <domain>`. `<path>` is a directory, or one HTML file published as index.html. The first run asks for an email and password, which creates the account.
- Static files only: build first, then publish the output directory (dist, build, _site, public).
- Without prompts (CI, agents): mint a token with `surge tokens add --domain <domain>`, then pass `--token <token>` to any command. The `SURGE_TOKEN` environment variable works too, and keeps the token out of shell history and logs. See https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation
- With no token and no terminal, the CLI aborts on stderr (`Aborted - not logged in and no terminal to ask.`) and exits 1. `surge whoami` shows the token's id and scope, and exits 1 when the credentials don't work.
- Previews: `surge <path> <domain> --preview` uploads a revision without touching production and prints its URL; `surge <domain> cutover <rev>` ships it. See https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews
- New accounts: `*.surge.sh` domains serve for 90 minutes, then report `ready` until the account's email is verified (`surge verify`). Nothing to republish after verifying.
- Limits: publishing is rate limited per domain, account and IP; a rate-limited publish answers 429 with `retry-after`. Projects are capped at 10,100 files and 450 MB. See https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#publishing-limits
- Everything the CLI does goes through the HTTP API, also usable from Node with surge-sdk.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/getting-started

# Getting Started

Surge publishes static web projects—HTML, CSS, and JavaScript—straight from the command line. This walkthrough takes you from nothing to a live project in about a minute.

## 1. Install the CLI

Surge runs on [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) (version 18 or later). With Node installed, grab the CLI from npm:

```sh
npm install --global surge
```

(If npm complains about permissions, [fix npm's global prefix or use a Node version manager](https://docs.npmjs.com/resolving-eacces-permissions-errors-when-installing-packages-globally) rather than reaching for `sudo`.)

## 2. Publish something

Go to any directory with an `index.html` in it—or make one:

```sh
mkdir lucid-example && cd lucid-example
echo '<h1>Hello, Surge</h1>' > index.html
surge publish
```

The first run asks you to create an account—just an email and password, right in the terminal. Then it prompts for the project (your current directory) and a domain, suggesting one based on your directory's name—accept it, or type anything you like:

```
$ surge publish

   Running as you@example.com (Free)

        project: /Users/you/lucid-example/
        project: /Users/sintaxi/Documents/Surge/steno/fixtures/lucid-example/dist
         domain: lucid-example.surge.sh
           size: 3 files, 672 bytes
         upload: [=========================] 100%
            CDN: [=========================] 100%
     encryption: [=========================] 100%

  ┌──────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │   CERT   │   *.surge.sh, surge.sh                                         │   auto-renew          │
  ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │   DNS    │   using Surge Name Servers                                     │   geo-aware           │
  └──────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘
  ┌──────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────┬─────────┐
  │   HTTP   │   sfo.surge.sh   │   US, San Francisco   │   138.197.235.123   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   lhr.surge.sh   │   GB, London          │   46.101.67.123     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   yyz.surge.sh   │   CA, Toronto         │   159.203.50.177    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   jfk.surge.sh   │   US, New York        │   159.203.159.100   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   ams.surge.sh   │   NL, Amsterdam       │   188.166.132.94    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   fra.surge.sh   │   DE, Frankfurt       │   138.68.112.220    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   sgp.surge.sh   │   SG, Singapore       │   139.59.195.30     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   blr.surge.sh   │   IN, Bangalore       │   139.59.50.135     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   syd.surge.sh   │   AU, Sydney          │   45.76.126.95      │   Vultr     │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   nrt.surge.sh   │   JP, Tokyo           │   172.104.96.133    │   Linode    │   ✔ ◍   │
  └──────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────┴─────────┘
   Live preview ................................................ 1785787164375--lucid-example.surge.sh
   Latest ............................................................. latest--lucid-example.surge.sh
   Production ................................................................. lucid-example.surge.sh

   Success! - Published to lucid-example.surge.sh

   domain written to CNAME
```

That's the entire flow. Your project is live on Surge's [CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn), over HTTPS, with [clean URLs](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/clean-urls)—at the domain you accepted or typed at the prompt.

**Verify your email.** A new account's `surge.sh` domains serve for their first 90 minutes; after that they wait—status **ready**—until the account's email address is verified, then serve again with nothing to republish. Run `surge verify` to get the link.

## 3. The domain is remembered

Notice the last line: the CLI wrote the domain to a `CNAME` file in your project, so every command now knows where the project lives. From now on `surge publish` ships straight there, no questions asked.

## 4. Ship an update

Change a file and run `surge publish` again. Each publish creates a new [revision](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions), and production cuts over atomically when the upload completes. Shipped a mistake? Undo it:

```sh
surge rollback
```

## Where to go from here

**Use your own domain.** Point it at Surge and publish—custom domains are free, and the SSL certificate is provisioned automatically. → [Custom Domains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains)

**Preview before you ship.** `surge publish --preview` uploads a revision with its own URL, without touching production. → [Previews](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews)

**Publish from CI.** Mint a token with `surge tokens add`, set `SURGE_TOKEN` in your pipeline, done. → [CI & Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation)

**Publishing a single-page app?** Name your shell `200.html` so deep links work. → [Client-Side Routing](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/spa-routing)

**Publishing a Vite, Astro, or Eleventy build?** The [Guides](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/) cover each framework's particulars—and migrating from GitHub Pages or Netlify.

Or head to the [CLI docs](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/) for the full tour of what `surge` can do.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/agents

# Surge for Coding Agents

This page is written for coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, OpenCode and the like) and for the people who run them. It is the complete, tested workflow for publishing a project to Surge without a human at the keyboard. It is also served as markdown: request this URL with `Accept: text/markdown`, or fetch [/docs/agents.md](https://surge.sh/docs/agents.md).

Surge puts a directory of static files on the web: `surge <path> <domain>`. There is no config file, no dashboard and no build step on Surge's side. Everything below is a command.

## The short version

```sh
# 1. build (the project's own build command)
npm run build

# 2. publish a preview: production does not change
SURGE_TOKEN=<token> npx surge@latest ./dist my-app.surge.sh --preview

# 3. report the preview URL to the human, then, only when they approve:
SURGE_TOKEN=<token> npx surge@latest my-app.surge.sh cutover <rev>
```

Rules that keep this safe:

- **Publish previews by default.** Move production only when the human has said so for this change.
- **Use the token you were given.** Never run `surge login`, and never type an email or password into the CLI on someone's behalf: logging in with an unknown email creates a new account.
- **Never print the token.** Don't echo `SURGE_TOKEN`, and don't run `surge token`, which prints the token in use.
- **Ask before anything destructive.** `teardown`, `discard`, `rem`, `nuke`, `dns rem`, `ssl` changes and collaborator changes all need explicit permission.
- **Don't pick a domain the human didn't name.** If the publish is refused because the domain belongs to another account, stop and ask.

## 1. Is the project deployable?

Surge serves static files: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, fonts, media, JSON, WebAssembly. It does not run server code, serverless functions, databases or builds.

A project fits Surge if its build writes a directory of static files, or if it already is one (an `index.html` at the root). It does not fit if it needs a server at request time: Next.js without `output: "export"`, SvelteKit or Nuxt without a static adapter, Express, Rails, Django, PHP. Say so instead of publishing a broken app.

## 2. Find the output directory

Build with the project's own command, then publish the directory it writes:

| Project | Build | Publish |
|---|---|---|
| Vite (React, Vue, Svelte, Solid) | `npm run build` | `./dist` |
| Astro (static output) | `npm run build` | `./dist` |
| Create React App | `npm run build` | `./build` |
| Next.js with `output: "export"` | `npm run build` | `./out` |
| SvelteKit with `adapter-static` | `npm run build` | `./build` |
| Nuxt (`nuxt generate`) | `npm run generate` | `./.output/public` |
| Angular | `npm run build` | `./dist/<project>/browser` |
| Eleventy | `npx @11ty/eleventy` | `./_site` |
| Hugo | `hugo` | `./public` |
| Jekyll | `bundle exec jekyll build` | `./_site` |
| VitePress | `npm run docs:build` | `./docs/.vitepress/dist` |
| Docusaurus | `npm run build` | `./build` |
| Plain HTML | none | `.` |
| One HTML file | none | `./page.html` (published as `index.html`) |

When in doubt, read the build config (`vite.config.*`, `astro.config.*`, `outDir`, `publishDir`) and check that the directory contains an `index.html` after the build.

Dotfiles and `node_modules` are never uploaded. That includes `.well-known/`. A project can be up to 450 MB and 10,100 files.

**Single-page apps** with client-side routing need a `200.html`, so that deep links serve the app instead of a 404:

```sh
cp dist/index.html dist/200.html
```

Add it after the build, every time, since builds clear the output directory. See [Client-Side Routing](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/spa-routing).

## 3. Install or invoke the CLI

```sh
npx surge@latest --version   # no install, Node 18 or newer
npm install --global surge   # or install once
```

Use `npx surge@latest` rather than bare `npx surge`: npx reuses whatever version it cached last time, which can be months old. Pin a version instead (`npx surge@0.48`) when you need reproducible runs.

## 4. Authenticate

Surge reads credentials in this order: the `--token` flag, then the `SURGE_TOKEN` environment variable, then a saved login. For agents, use `SURGE_TOKEN`: it keeps the token out of the command line and the transcript.

The human creates the token, once, scoped to the domain the agent may publish:

```sh
surge tokens add --domain my-app.surge.sh -m "coding agent"
```

A scoped token works only on that domain: it can publish, preview, roll back and also tear the domain down, but it can't touch the account, other domains, DNS, collaborators or billing. Repeat `--domain` to allow several. Without `--domain` a token has full account access, which is more than an agent needs. The human can list and remove tokens with `surge tokens` and `surge tokens rem <id>`.

Check what you were given before you publish:

```sh
surge whoami
```

With a token, `whoami` prints the account, the token's id and its scope. With no valid credentials it exits non-zero. Don't proceed if it fails, and ask the human for a token.

**Without a terminal, the CLI never waits for input.** If there are no credentials it prints `` Aborted - not logged in and no terminal to ask. Run `surge login` in a terminal, or set SURGE_TOKEN. `` to stderr and exits 1. Pass the path and the domain explicitly every time so that nothing else would need asking.

## 5. Publish a preview

```sh
npx surge@latest ./dist my-app.surge.sh --preview
```

A preview uploads a new revision of the domain and gives it its own address, without changing what the domain serves. On success the last line is:

```txt
   Success! - Preview available at 1785787164375--my-app.surge.sh
```

- The preview URL is `https://` plus that host. For a custom domain like `example.com` it looks like `https://1785787164375--example--com.surge.sh`.
- The number before the first `--` is the **revision id**. You need it to promote this exact build.
- Report the URL to the human with what changed. Don't promote it yourself.

Check the exit code as well as the output: 0 means the publish succeeded, anything else means it didn't. Previews count toward the [rate limits](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#publishing-limits) like any publish.

If the domain has never been published, the human may prefer a straight first publish (step 6) since there's no production to protect. Ask.

## 6. Publish to production, when authorized

Promote the revision the human approved, by id:

```sh
npx surge@latest my-app.surge.sh cutover 1785787164375
```

Always pass the id. A bare `cutover` promotes the latest revision, which may not be the one that was reviewed if anything else published in between.

A direct production publish, when the human asked for one, is the same command as the preview without `--preview`:

```sh
npx surge@latest ./dist my-app.surge.sh
```

```txt
   Success! - Published to my-app.surge.sh
```

Publishes and previews write the domain to a `CNAME` file in the published directory, so later commands know where the project lives. Keep passing the domain explicitly anyway: a stale `CNAME` points a bare `surge ./dist publish` at the wrong domain.

## 7. Verify

```sh
npx surge@latest my-app.surge.sh status   # domain status: live, securing, waiting on dns, ready
npx surge@latest my-app.surge.sh revs     # the revisions this domain keeps
curl -sI https://my-app.surge.sh   # what visitors get
```

A `*.surge.sh` domain is live over HTTPS as soon as the publish returns. New `*.surge.sh` domains redirect HTTP to HTTPS by default, which is the `force: https` line in the publish output. A custom domain serves once its DNS points at Surge. See [Custom Domains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains) for the records, and don't change DNS without the human.

`ready` means the domain belongs to a new account whose email isn't verified yet: it served for its first 90 minutes and is paused until the human clicks the link in their welcome email (or runs `surge verify`). Tell the human; there's nothing for the agent to fix.

## 8. Recover

Roll back to the previous revision, when the human asks or when a production publish you made is broken:

```sh
npx surge@latest my-app.surge.sh rollback
```

`rollfore` moves forward again, and `cutover <rev>` jumps to any revision. Nothing is uploaded, so all three are instant. The last 100 revisions are kept. See [Revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions).

What the errors mean:

| Output | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `Aborted - not logged in and no terminal to ask` | No credentials | Ask the human for a token. Don't log in. |
| `Invalid token` | Token wrong, removed, or expired | Ask the human for a new one. |
| `Aborted - you do not have permission to publish to <domain>` | Another account owns the domain, or the token is scoped to a different one | Stop and ask. Don't try other domains on your own. |
| `Aborted - Rate limited. (domain). Try again in 9 hours.` | A publishing limit was hit | Stop. Retrying while limited extends the limit. Report when it resets. |
| `Project too large - the limit is 450 MB` | Over the size cap | Check you're publishing the build output, not the repository. |
| A prompt to upgrade, or an `AUTH`/`ROUTER` error | The project uses a Pro feature | Ask the human; upgrading is their decision. |
| `Aborted - '<word>' is not a surge argument` | A flag that doesn't exist | Check the [command reference](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/reference). |

## Install the skill

The steps above are packaged as an [Agent Skill](https://agentskills.io) named `deploy-to-surge`, so agents that support skills load the workflow when it's relevant:

```sh
npx skills add https://surge.sh/skills/deploy-to-surge/SKILL.md
```

Or copy [SKILL.md](https://surge.sh/skills/deploy-to-surge/SKILL.md) into your agent's skills directory (`.claude/skills/deploy-to-surge/`, `.agents/skills/deploy-to-surge/`, and so on).

## Add Surge to AGENTS.md

To make Surge the deploy target for a repository, paste this into its `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`) and fill in the domain and output directory:

```md
## Deploying

This project publishes to Surge: https://surge.sh/docs/agents

- Build: `npm run build` (output in `./dist`)
- Preview: `npx surge@latest ./dist my-app.surge.sh --preview`, then report the preview URL
- Production: only when asked, `npx surge@latest my-app.surge.sh cutover <rev>` with the preview's revision id
- Credentials come from `SURGE_TOKEN`. Never log in, never print the token.
- Ask before teardown, discard, DNS or collaborator changes.
```

## More

- [CI & Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation): tokens in CI, GitHub Actions previews per pull request
- [Previews](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews) and [Revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions)
- [Command reference](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/reference)
- [llms.txt](https://surge.sh/llms.txt) indexes every docs page; [llms-full.txt](https://surge.sh/llms-full.txt) has them all in one file

# The Surge CLI

`surge` is a command line tool for publishing static web projects. It does one thing exceptionally well—putting a directory on the web—and then gives you everything you need to run it in production: custom domains, SSL, instant rollbacks, DNS, teams, and analytics, all without leaving the terminal.

## Install

```sh
npm install --global surge
```

Requires [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 18 or later. No account setup beforehand—the CLI walks you through creating one on first publish. See [Getting Started](https://surge.sh/docs/getting-started) for the full walkthrough.

## The whole surface

Everything the CLI does fits on one screen:

```
$ surge --help

  Surge.sh ⚡ Static Web Publishing 0.53.0

  PUBLISHING
    surge <path> <domain>                 publish dir to domain
    surge <path> publish                  publish using local CNAME
    surge <page.html> <domain>            publish one html page as index.html
    surge <path> <domain> --preview       publish a preview, production untouched

  REVISIONS
    surge <domain> revs                   list revisions
    surge <domain> cutover [<rev>]        serve a revision (ships a preview)
    surge <domain> rollback|rollfore      change live revision
    surge <domain> discard <rev>          remove a revision

  ADMIN
    surge whoami                          display current session
    surge login                           authenticate
    surge logout                          remove session & expire token
    surge verify                          verify email address
    surge mfa                             manage two-factor auth
    surge list                            list your domains, newest first
    surge card                            change billing credit card
    surge plan                            show/change account plan
    surge tokens                          show available tokens commands
    surge orgs                            show your orgs
    surge claim <code>                    join an org, or take a domain, with a code
    surge scrap <code>                    cancel an invite or transfer code

  PROJECT
    surge <domain> config                 show/change project configuration
    surge <domain> transfer [<org>]       move to an org, or get a code to give it away
    surge <domain> teardown               remove project (!destructive)
    surge <domain> stats                  show available analytics commands
    surge <domain> dns                    show available dns commands
    surge <domain> debug                  show available debug commands

  AUTH
    --token <token>                       authenticate without logging in
    SURGE_TOKEN=<token>                   same, from the environment

  surge <command> --help for one command
```

That's the design constraint the whole tool is built under: a surface small enough to hold in your head, arranged so the command you need is the command you'd guess.

## The grammar

Every project command names its target first, then the verb:

```sh
surge <project> <verb>
```

The project is a **domain** (`example.com`), a **path** (`./dist`), or—when omitted—the **current directory**. So these are the same command at three levels of explicitness:

```sh
surge example.com rollback     # the domain, spelled out
surge ./dist rollback          # a project directory that knows its domain
surge rollback                 # the current directory's project
```

Day to day you work from inside your project, so the short forms carry you: `surge publish`, `surge revs`, `surge rollback`. The explicit forms exist for scripts, CI, and operating on projects you're not standing in.

Two safety properties fall out of the grammar. A target with no verb never acts—`surge example.com`, or just `surge`, prints an overview instead of doing something to production. And commands typed in the older, verb-first order (`surge rollback example.com`) keep working forever, silently—both orders are first-class. Muscle memory is never punished.

## Design principles

**Publishing is global, and it's done when it says it's done.** A publish doesn't upload to "a server" and trickle outward—it propagates to every edge node of [Surge's CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) while the command runs, and the output confirms each node individually. When you see `Success!`, your project is live in every region, not queued for it. That's also why [rollback](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) is instant: moving between revisions is a pointer switch, not a re-upload.

**The prompt is the UI.** Anything the CLI needs and doesn't have, it asks for—and every prompt can be pre-empted with an argument or flag, so every workflow scripts cleanly. `surge ./dist example.com` never asks a question. There is no dashboard you'll eventually be forced into; the terminal is the whole product.

**Your project is the configuration.** The domain lives in a [`CNAME` file](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#the-cname-file). Files to exclude go in [`.surgeignore`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#ignoring-files). Server behavior—[auth](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth), [redirects](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/redirects), [CORS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cors)—is plain files that publish with your code. There's no manifest, no scaffolding, no project state living anywhere but your directory. Every [revision](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) therefore carries its complete configuration: roll back the code and the behavior rolls back with it.

**Publishing is cheap and reversible.** Every publish creates an immutable revision with its own preview URL, and Surge keeps the last 100 of them. Ship freely—the previous version is one `surge rollback` away, effective everywhere instantly. The cost of a mistake is a command, which changes how boldly you ship.

## The command surface

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `surge <path> <domain>` | [Publish a project to a domain](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing) |
| `surge <path> publish` | [Publish using the project's `CNAME` file](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#the-cname-file) |
| `surge … --preview` | [Publish a preview without touching production](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews) |
| `surge <domain> revs` | [List a project's revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) |
| `surge <domain> rollback` / `rollfore` / `cutover` / `discard` | [Move between revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) |
| `surge <domain> dns` / `zone` | [Manage DNS records](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/domains) |
| `surge <domain> stats` | [Traffic, audience, usage, and load](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics) |
| `surge <domain> status` | [Where the domain stands: waiting on dns, securing, ready, or live](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics#status) |
| `surge <domain> debug` | [Status, files, audit, cache, certificates](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics#debug) |
| `surge <domain> config` | [View and change project settings](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config) |
| `surge <domain> transfer` / `surge claim` | [Move a domain into an org, or give it to someone](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#moving-a-domain) |
| `surge orgs` | [Share domains as a team](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams), [create orgs, manage members and tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs) |
| `surge <domain> teardown` | [Remove a published project](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions#tearing-down-a-project) |
| `surge list` | Your domains and your orgs', newest first |
| `surge login` / `logout` / `whoami` / `verify` / `plan` / `card` / `tokens` / `nuke` | [Account, plans & tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account) |

The complete listing with every flag is in the [Command Reference](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/reference)—or run `surge --help`, which adapts to the project you run it in: inside a project directory the target slot fills in, and the screen shows exactly the commands you can run right there. For one command's usage, run `surge <command> --help` (for example `surge cutover --help`).

## Where to go

New to Surge? [Getting Started](https://surge.sh/docs/getting-started) has you live in about a minute. Publishing a Vite, Astro, or Eleventy build—or migrating from another host? The [Guides](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/) walk each task end to end. Shipping to production? [Publishing](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing), [Previews](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews), and [Revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) are the working loop. Automating? [CI & Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation) covers tokens and pipelines. And everything about how the platform serves what you publish lives in the [Platform docs](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/).

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing

# Publishing

Publishing takes a directory and puts it on the web at a domain:

```sh
surge <path> <domain>
```

```
$ surge ./dist lucid-example.surge.sh

   Running as you@example.com (Free)

        project: ./dist
         domain: lucid-example.surge.sh
           size: 3 files, 672 bytes
         upload: [=========================] 100%
            CDN: [=========================] 100%
     encryption: [=========================] 100%

  ┌──────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │   CERT   │   *.surge.sh, surge.sh                                         │   auto-renew          │
  ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │   DNS    │   using Surge Name Servers                                     │   geo-aware           │
  └──────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘
  ┌──────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────┬─────────┐
  │   HTTP   │   sfo.surge.sh   │   US, San Francisco   │   138.197.235.123   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   lhr.surge.sh   │   GB, London          │   46.101.67.123     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   yyz.surge.sh   │   CA, Toronto         │   159.203.50.177    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   jfk.surge.sh   │   US, New York        │   159.203.159.100   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   ams.surge.sh   │   NL, Amsterdam       │   188.166.132.94    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   fra.surge.sh   │   DE, Frankfurt       │   138.68.112.220    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   sgp.surge.sh   │   SG, Singapore       │   139.59.195.30     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   blr.surge.sh   │   IN, Bangalore       │   139.59.50.135     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   syd.surge.sh   │   AU, Sydney          │   45.76.126.95      │   Vultr     │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   nrt.surge.sh   │   JP, Tokyo           │   172.104.96.133    │   Linode    │   ✔ ◍   │
  └──────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────┴─────────┘
   Live preview ................................................ 1785787164375--lucid-example.surge.sh
   Latest ............................................................. latest--lucid-example.surge.sh
   Production ................................................................. lucid-example.surge.sh

   Success! - Published to lucid-example.surge.sh

   domain written to dist/CNAME
```

Every publish reports the whole picture: the certificate covering the domain, how DNS is answered, and each edge node of the [CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) confirming what it serves—plus the revision's permanent preview URL and the domain's [latest URL](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews#the-latest-url) alongside production.

Some useful forms:

```sh
surge ./dist example.com       # publish ./dist to example.com — no prompts
surge . example.com            # publish the current directory
surge ./dist _                 # publish to a fresh generated .surge.sh domain
surge page.html example.com    # publish one HTML page as the domain's index.html
surge ./dist publish           # publish using the project's CNAME file
surge publish                  # same, from inside the project directory
surge -p ./dist -d example.com # flag form, for pipelines
```

`surge <path> publish` is the constructor: run against a directory that has never been published, it prompts for the domain—suggesting a generated `.surge.sh` subdomain you can accept, replace with any domain you own, or refresh by typing `_`. Once the project knows its domain (see [the CNAME file](#the-cname-file)), the same command publishes with no questions at all.

## A single HTML file

Pass a file instead of a directory and the page is published on its own, as the domain's `index.html`:

```sh
surge page.html my-page.surge.sh
```

- **The domain.** Run without one, the prompt suggests a name from the file: `page.html` suggests `page.surge.sh`, and an `index.html` suggests its folder's name.
- **HTML only.** `.html` and `.htm` files publish this way. Anything else is refused before the upload starts—put it in a folder and publish the folder.
- **The page goes up alone.** If it uses images, stylesheets, or scripts sitting next to it, the output names them as `left behind`. Publish the folder to include them.
- **No CNAME file.** A single file never takes its domain from a `CNAME` in the current directory (that belongs to another project), and none is written. Pass the domain every time.
- **It replaces the domain.** Like any publish, the page becomes the whole of what the domain serves.

This needs surge 0.45 or newer; `npm install -g surge` updates it.

## Choosing a domain

You can publish to two kinds of domain:

- **A `surge.sh` subdomain** — free, instant, no setup: `anything-you-like.surge.sh`, as long as it's not taken.
- **Your own domain** — also free; point it at Surge first. See [Domains & DNS](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/domains).

The `--force` flag controls HTTPS behavior: publish with `surge ./dist example.com --force https` and the platform will redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS (new `.surge.sh` subdomains start out that way). Add `--private` to lock the domain to the people who can publish it, or `--public` to open it again—see [private domains](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config#private-domains). More in [SSL & HTTPS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl).

## The CNAME file

A project remembers its domain in a file named `CNAME` at the root of the directory you publish—and Surge writes it for you. That's the `domain written to dist/CNAME` line in the output above: publish to a domain once, and the project knows where it lives. From then on `surge publish` goes straight there with no prompt—and every other command resolves its target the same way, so `surge rollback` or `surge dns list` inside the project just work.

The convention is shared with GitHub Pages, so a project can move between the two without changes. One thing to know if a build tool generates the directory you publish: the next build may wipe the file with everything else—the [framework guides](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/) show where to keep it so it survives.

## Ignoring files

By default, Surge excludes things that don't belong on a web server:

```txt
.git  .*  *.*~  node_modules  bower_components
```

To exclude more, add a `.surgeignore` file to your project root. It uses the same syntax as `.gitignore`:

```gitignore
# .surgeignore
src/
*.map
drafts/
```

The `.*` rule excludes every dot-directory, `.well-known/` included. To publish one, re-include it with a negated line:

```gitignore
# .surgeignore
!.well-known
```

Everything else in the directory is published. Before uploading, the CLI prints a `size:` line with the file count and total size, so you'll notice if something unexpected is being included. Projects are limited to 10,100 files and 450 MB; a larger project is refused before anything is published.

## Messages

Attach a message to a publish the way you would to a git commit. Messages show up in the revision list, which makes `surge <domain> revs` read like a log of everything you've shipped:

```sh
surge publish -m "fix nav on mobile"
```

## Publishing limits

There's no cap on how many projects or domains you publish, but how often you publish is rate limited. Limits are counted over rolling windows:

| Limit | Per 15 minutes | Per 24 hours |
|-------|----------------|--------------|
| Each domain | 30 | 200 |
| Each account | 60 | 500 |
| Each IP address | 240 | — |

Accounts with an unverified email get half of each limit—run `surge verify` to lift them (see [account](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account)). [Previews](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews) count the same as publishes.

When you go over, the publish aborts with the limit you hit and when to try again:

```txt
Aborted - Rate limited. (domain). Try again in 9 hours.
```

Attempts made while limited count toward the window too, so a job that keeps retrying stays limited. Stop and resume after the time shown. For scheduled or looping jobs, the 24-hour limit is the one to plan around: 200 a day is one publish every ~7 minutes, so publish every 10 minutes or more—or better, only when the content has changed. See [CI & Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation).

## What happens on publish

A publish is done when it says it's done—everywhere. Your files upload once, then propagate to **every edge node of [Surge's CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) while the command runs**; the `CDN:` bar is that propagation happening, and the table underneath is each node individually confirming what it now serves. There's no "allow a few minutes for changes to appear," no cache to wait out: when `Success!` prints, the new revision is live in every region at once.

Only changed files travel. For projects over 1 MB, files the domain's live revision already has are carried over rather than uploaded again, so republishing a large project with a small change is quick.

The cutover is atomic. Every publish creates a new [revision](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) (Surge keeps the last 100), and production points at it only after the upload completes—a failed or interrupted publish leaves the live project exactly as it was. To upload without moving production at all, use a [preview](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews).

The output also reports the state of the domain itself—the certificate covering it, how DNS is answered, and the exact records to add if the domain isn't pointing at Surge yet.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews

# Previews

A preview uploads a new revision **without changing what production serves**. You get a URL to check, share, and test against—and production stays exactly as it was until you decide otherwise.

```sh
surge publish --preview
```

```
$ surge ./dist publish --preview

   Running as you@example.com (Free)

        project: ./dist
         domain: lucid-example.surge.sh
           size: 4 files, 695 bytes
         upload: [=========================] 100%
            CDN: [=========================] 100%
     encryption: [=========================] 100%

  ┌──────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │   CERT   │   *.surge.sh, surge.sh                                         │   auto-renew          │
  ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │   DNS    │   using Surge Name Servers                                     │   geo-aware           │
  └──────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘
  ┌──────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────┬─────────┐
  │   HTTP   │   sfo.surge.sh   │   US, San Francisco   │   138.197.235.123   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   lhr.surge.sh   │   GB, London          │   46.101.67.123     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   yyz.surge.sh   │   CA, Toronto         │   159.203.50.177    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   jfk.surge.sh   │   US, New York        │   159.203.159.100   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   ams.surge.sh   │   NL, Amsterdam       │   188.166.132.94    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   fra.surge.sh   │   DE, Frankfurt       │   138.68.112.220    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   sgp.surge.sh   │   SG, Singapore       │   139.59.195.30     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   blr.surge.sh   │   IN, Bangalore       │   139.59.50.135     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   syd.surge.sh   │   AU, Sydney          │   45.76.126.95      │   Vultr     │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   nrt.surge.sh   │   JP, Tokyo           │   172.104.96.133    │   Linode    │   ✔ ◍   │
  └──────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────┴─────────┘
   Live preview ................................................ 1785787164375--lucid-example.surge.sh
   Latest ............................................................. latest--lucid-example.surge.sh

   Success! - Preview available at 1785787164375--lucid-example.surge.sh
```

(`--stage` and `-s` are aliases for `--preview`.)

## The preview URL

Every revision—previewed or published—gets a URL of its own, served over the same CDN as production: the preview propagates to [every edge node](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) just like a real publish, so what you're checking is exactly what production will be, served exactly how production serves.

The host is built from the revision id and the domain:

| Domain | Preview host |
|--------|--------------|
| A `surge.sh` subdomain, e.g. `example.surge.sh` | `1785787164375--example.surge.sh` |
| Your own domain, e.g. `example.com` | `1785787164375--example--com.surge.sh` |

Previews of a custom domain live under `surge.sh`, so they work—over HTTPS—whatever your DNS points at, even before the domain itself is live. The URL lasts as long as the revision does (Surge keeps the last 100 per domain), so it works for:

- **Review**: send the link to a teammate or client before shipping.
- **Testing**: point integration tests at the exact bits that will go live.
- **History**: recent revisions stay viewable at their own URLs, listed by `surge <domain> revs`.

Preview hosts read as `<revision>--<domain>.surge.sh`: a domain one level under `surge.sh` is written as its name, any other domain in full with each dot written as `--`. Links in the older forms (`1785787164375-example.surge.sh`, `1785787164375--example-com.surge.sh`) keep working.

## The latest URL

Put `latest` where the revision id goes and the URL always shows the domain's newest revision, previewed or published:

| Domain | Latest host |
|--------|-------------|
| `example.surge.sh` | `latest--example.surge.sh` |
| `example.com` | `latest--example--com.surge.sh` |

Every publish prints it on the `Latest` line. It moves on the next preview or publish, and falls back to the one before when a revision is discarded—so it is the link to hand a reviewer or put in a PR template once, and keep. To show one exact build, use the revision's own URL.

Anyone who knows the domain can guess its latest URL, so a preview is only as private as the domain: work that must stay unseen until launch belongs on a [`--private`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config#private-domains) domain or behind an [AUTH](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth) file. Preview and latest URLs enforce both, and never get indexed by search engines.

## Shipping a preview

When the preview looks right, cut it over to production:

```sh
surge example.com cutover
```

`cutover` points production at the latest revision—the one you just previewed. Nothing is re-uploaded; the switch is atomic. If you previewed several candidates, pass the specific revision to ship:

```sh
surge example.com cutover 1719852000000
```

If the preview *isn't* right, discard it and production never knew it existed:

```sh
surge example.com discard 1719852000000
```

## A typical flow

```sh
surge publish --preview -m "redesigned pricing page"   # upload a candidate
# …check the preview URL, share it, run tests…
surge cutover                                          # ship it
```

This is also the natural shape for CI: every branch build publishes a preview, and merging to the main branch runs a plain publish (or a `cutover`). See [CI & Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation).

For the full picture of how revisions work—rollback, rollfore, discard—see [Revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions).

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions

# Revisions

Every publish creates a revision—a complete, immutable snapshot of your project with its own [preview URL](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews#the-preview-url). Surge keeps the last 100 revisions of each domain; older ones drop off as new ones arrive. Production is just a pointer at one of them, and the revision commands move that pointer. Shipped something broken? You're one command from the previous version.

## Listing revisions

`surge list` shows your domains and your orgs', newest first. `revs` shows one project's revisions, newest last:

```
$ surge vivid-example.surge.sh revs

  1785786900000--vivid-example.surge.sh  Just now  you@example.com  4 files  695.0B  new hero section
  1785787164375--vivid-example.surge.sh  Just now  you@example.com  4 files  695.0B  fix nav on mobile
```

The revision currently serving production is highlighted. Each row shows the revision's preview URL, its age, who published it, its size, and the [message](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#messages)—write good messages and this becomes a log of everything you've shipped. (Inside a project directory, plain `surge revs` does the same.)

## Moving between revisions

```sh
surge example.com rollback    # serve the previous revision
surge example.com rollfore    # serve the next revision
surge example.com cutover     # serve the latest revision
```

```
$ surge vivid-example.surge.sh rollback

   ⟲ Rollback

  1785786900000--vivid-example.surge.sh    /└───   1785787164375--vivid-example.surge.sh   
  by you@example.com              /        by you@example.com              
  4 files, 695 size                       \        4 files, 695 size                       
  Tue, 04 Aug 2026 02:35:00 GMT            \┌───   Tue, 04 Aug 2026 02:39:24 GMT           

  ┌──────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          │   ns1.surge.world   ns2.surge.world     or CNAME…                                      │
  │    NS    │   ns3.surge.world   ns4.surge.world     geo.surge.world                                │
  ├──────────┼──────────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────┬─────────┤
  │   HTTP   │   sfo.surge.sh   │   US, San Francisco   │   138.197.235.123   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   lhr.surge.sh   │   GB, London          │   46.101.67.123     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   yyz.surge.sh   │   CA, Toronto         │   159.203.50.177    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   jfk.surge.sh   │   US, New York        │   159.203.159.100   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   ams.surge.sh   │   NL, Amsterdam       │   188.166.132.94    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   fra.surge.sh   │   DE, Frankfurt       │   138.68.112.220    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   sgp.surge.sh   │   SG, Singapore       │   139.59.195.30     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   blr.surge.sh   │   IN, Bangalore       │   139.59.50.135     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   syd.surge.sh   │   AU, Sydney          │   45.76.126.95      │   Vultr     │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   nrt.surge.sh   │   JP, Tokyo           │   172.104.96.133    │   Linode    │   ✔ ◍   │
  └──────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────┴─────────┘

   Done! - vivid-example.surge.sh now serving revision 1785786900000--vivid-example.surge.sh
```

The two cards are the revisions production is moving between—the pointer steps from the newer to the older—and the table confirms the change across the network, ending with the revision now serving.

- **`rollback`** steps production one revision back. Run it again to go back further.
- **`rollfore`** steps production one revision forward—the undo for a rollback.
- **`cutover`** jumps production to the latest revision, or to a specific one: `surge example.com cutover 1719765600000`. This is how a [preview](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews) ships.

All three are pointer moves, and that's why they're instant: every revision is already stored on the platform, so moving production between them uploads nothing and rebuilds nothing—the pointer switches across [every edge node](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn), worldwide, in the time it takes the command to run. Shipped something broken at the worst possible moment? The fix is faster than the panic. If the pointer is already where you asked it to go, the command reports `Unchanged` and does nothing.

Note that publishing normally cuts over automatically: a rolled-back project that receives a fresh publish will serve the new revision. To upload without cutting over, use `--preview`.

## Discarding revisions

Remove a revision from the system entirely:

```sh
surge example.com discard 1719852000000
```

If the discarded revision was serving production, production moves to a neighboring revision (the CLI reports which way it went). Discard the only revision and the project goes offline.

## Tearing down a project

To take a project down completely—every revision, gone from every edge node:

```
$ surge vivid-example.surge.sh teardown

   Success - vivid-example.surge.sh has been removed.
```

Teardown removes the project from your account. It doesn't touch DNS records or your domain registration, so republishing to the same domain later works exactly like the first publish.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/domains

# Domains & DNS

Custom domains are free on Surge. Publish to one the same way you'd publish to a subdomain:

```sh
surge ./dist example.com
```

For the domain to resolve, it has to point at Surge—by delegating to Surge's name servers, a `CNAME` record, or an `A` record. The records, the trade-offs between the three, and the domain's states (**waiting on dns** → **securing** → **live**) are all in [Custom Domains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains). Until the domain points at Surge, every publish prints the exact records to add; check where things stand any time with [`surge <domain> status`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics#status).

This page covers the CLI side: the DNS records Surge answers for a delegated domain.

## Managing DNS records

Once a domain is delegated to Surge's name servers (`ns1`–`ns4.surge.world`, also printed by bare `surge <domain> dns`), the `dns` commands manage your custom records—no dashboard needed. This is how you keep email, subdomains, and verification records working on a domain that Surge serves:

```sh
surge example.com dns list                        # view records
surge example.com dns add <type> <name> <value>   # add a record
surge example.com dns rem <id>                    # remove a record
```

For example:

```sh
# Point a subdomain somewhere else
surge example.com dns add CNAME app app.example.dev

# Domain verification for a search console
surge example.com dns add TXT @ "google-site-verification=…"

# Mail — MX records take a priority before the value
surge example.com dns add MX 10 mail.example.com
surge example.com dns add MX @ 10 mail.example.com   # explicit host form
```

Adding or removing a record prints the resulting record set along with a `Success` confirmation. Each record has an id, shown in the listing, which is what `rem` takes.

DNS management applies to apex domains (`example.com`, not `sub.example.com`) that are delegated to Surge's name servers. Add your existing records *before* switching the name servers, and nothing skips a beat.

## Viewing the full zone

`dns list` shows the records *you've* added. To see everything Surge is answering for the domain—including the records it manages automatically—use `zone`:

```sh
surge example.com zone
```

This prints the domain's complete zone in BIND format: SOA, NS, and all records. `zone` also supports `add` and `rem` with the same syntax as `dns`, for the rare case where you need to override a managed record.

## Subdomains

Every subdomain is its own independent project—`surge ./docs docs.example.com`—with its own revisions, settings, and owner. See [Subdomains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains#subdomains) for what each DNS setup needs.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/ssl

# SSL Certificates

Every project on Surge is served over HTTPS, and custom domains get managed certificates automatically—there is no certificate step in the normal flow. How that works and forcing HTTPS are covered in [SSL & HTTPS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl).

This page covers the commands for watching that process and nudging it.

## Watching a domain go secure

```sh
surge example.com status
```

Reports **waiting on dns**, **securing**, or **live** (and **ready** for a new account's domains awaiting email verification)—see [Checking the status](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains#checking-the-status). Publishing reports the same states, so you rarely need to ask separately.

## Forcing HTTPS

```sh
surge ./dist example.com --force https     # at publish
surge example.com config --force https     # or as configuration, no publish
```

The setting sticks across publishes; `surge example.com config --force null` clears it. See [Forcing HTTPS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl#forcing-https).

## Inspecting certificates

```sh
surge example.com debug certs
```

Prints every certificate installed for the domain—subject, issuer, alternate names, expiry, and whether auto-renewal is on. To check certificate state on each individual edge node (useful when diagnosing propagation), see [`debug audit`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics#audit).

## Provisioning manually

```sh
surge example.com debug encrypt
```

`debug encrypt` asks the platform to provision the domain's managed certificate right now, streaming progress as it goes. Since certificates are provisioned and renewed automatically, you shouldn't need it day to day—it's the lever for unusual situations, like re-securing a domain after DNS was broken for a long stretch.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config

# Project Configuration

Every project carries a small set of platform settings—the knobs that control how the edge serves it. The `config` command views and changes them, and changes take effect across [every edge node](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) immediately: no republish, no cache to wait out.

## Viewing configuration

```sh
surge example.com config
```

Prints the project's current settings as `key: value` pairs. A fresh project has nothing set and prints `Empty`—every setting below is optional, and absence means the sensible default. (Inside a project directory, plain `surge config` does the same.)

## Changing configuration

Pass any setting as a flag; pass `null` to clear one back to its default:

```sh
surge example.com config --force https      # set
surge example.com config --force null       # clear
```

The command prints the resulting configuration so you can confirm exactly what's now in effect.

## The settings

| Setting | Values | What it controls |
|---------|--------|------------------|
| `force` | `http`, `https` | Redirect all traffic to one protocol. `https` is the right value for almost every project—publishing with `--force https` sets it for you. |
| `redirect` | a domain | Answer every request with a redirect to another domain—how a retired domain sends visitors to its successor. |
| `cors` | a domain, `*` | Allow cross-origin requests from one origin, or any. The [`CORS` file](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cors) does this per-project in code; the setting does it from the platform side. |
| `hsts` | seconds | Send a `Strict-Transport-Security` header with the given max-age, telling browsers to insist on HTTPS. |
| `private` | `true`, `false` | Require sign-in for the whole domain. The people who can publish it get in; everyone else meets the sign-in page, and crawlers get a `Disallow: /` robots.txt. The [`AUTH` file](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth) does this per-path. |

Every setting is available on every plan, `cors` and `private` included.

## Private domains

`private` also works as a flag at publish time—`surge ./dist example.com --private` publishes and locks the domain in one move, and `--public` flips it back:

```sh
surge example.com config --private     # lock the domain
surge example.com config --public      # open it again
```

A private domain serves only the people who can publish it: the members of the [org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams) that owns it, or you for a domain of your own, plus anyone [invited before orgs](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams#collaborators-from-before-orgs). Someone joining or leaving the org takes effect without a republish. Everything else about serving is unchanged: certs provision, previews work, and the domain stays live the whole time. When some paths should be open and others protected, or when specific outside people need in, that granularity lives in the [`AUTH` file](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth).

## Configuration from your project files

Most day-to-day behavior isn't set through `config` at all—it's driven by files in the directory you publish, which travel with every publish:

| File | Controls |
|------|----------|
| `CNAME` | The project's domain. See [Publishing](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#the-cname-file). |
| `.surgeignore` | Files excluded from publishing. See [Publishing](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#ignoring-files). |
| `AUTH` | Password protection and protected paths (Pro). See [the platform docs](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth). |
| `CORS` | Cross-origin resource sharing. See [CORS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cors). |
| `ROUTER` | Redirects and routing rules (Pro). See [Redirects](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/redirects). |
| `200.html` | Client-side routing for single-page apps. See [SPA routing](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/spa-routing). |
| `404.html` | The not-found page. See [Custom 404 pages](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-404). |

The split is deliberate: anything that should be versioned with your code lives *in* the project and rolls back with it, revision by revision. Anything about the running service—which revision is live, protocol enforcement, platform-side redirects—is `config`, applied to the domain no matter what's published there.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics

# Analytics & Diagnostics

Surge collects traffic analytics for every project at the edge—no script tag, no cookie banner, nothing added to your pages, nothing for your visitors to load—and renders them right in the terminal. The `stats` verbs answer the questions you actually ask about an audience; the `debug` verbs let you interrogate the platform node by node, because on a CDN "is it working?" is really ten questions with ten answers. All of them take the target first, and resolve it from the current directory when you're inside the project.

## Stats

### traffic

```sh
surge example.com stats traffic
```

The overview: a bar chart of unique visitors across the last two weeks, visits and connections with day-over-day deltas, the share of traffic arriving encrypted, cache hit rates—plus the day's most-visited pages, 404s, redirects, and referring sources.

### audience

```sh
surge example.com stats audience
```

Who's visiting: browsers, operating systems, and device types, with counts.

### usage

```sh
surge example.com stats usage
```

Bandwidth: per-file bytes served today and yesterday, with a projected monthly total—so you can see exactly which assets are heavy before they become a problem.

### load

```sh
surge example.com stats load
```

Connection volume charted per datacenter across the network. Useful for understanding where in the world your traffic lands.

---

## Debug

### status

```sh
surge example.com debug status
surge example.com status          # the same command
```

The state of the domain itself: **waiting on dns** (not pointing at Surge yet—the records to add are printed), **securing** (certificate being provisioned), **ready** (a new account's `surge.sh` domain, published and serving once the email is verified), or **live** (serving, verified against the edge). This is the first command to reach for when a domain isn't behaving; it tells you whose move it is. The states are explained on [Custom Domains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains#checking-the-status).

### files

```sh
surge example.com debug files
```

Lists every file in the live revision with its size—the manifest of exactly what the CDN is serving, as opposed to what's on your disk.

### audit

```sh
surge example.com debug audit
```

Asks every edge node what it's serving for the domain: the revision, file count, total size, and the state of its SSL certificate. If a publish or certificate seems inconsistent from where someone's sitting, `audit` shows you node by node whether the network agrees.

### bust

```sh
surge example.com debug bust
```

Purges the project from the cache on every edge node, forcing the next request to fetch fresh content. Publishing invalidates correctly on its own, so day to day you shouldn't need this—it's the "make absolutely sure" lever, and it prints which nodes confirmed the purge.

### certs & encrypt

`debug certs` inspects the certificates installed for the domain, and `debug encrypt` provisions the managed certificate manually. Both are covered in [SSL Certificates](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/ssl).

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams

# Teams

A team shares Surge through an [org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs). Everyone signs in as themselves and the org owns the domains, so nobody shares a password and nothing depends on one person's login. People come and go; the domains, their revisions and their settings stay with the org.

## Setting up

```sh
surge orgs acme create --name "Acme Inc."   # you're its admin
surge orgs acme invite                      # prints a code - one per teammate
```

Send each teammate their code, or the claim link printed under it. They join from their own account, whichever one they sign in with:

```sh
surge claim tiger73azqrk
```

The link (`https://auth.surge.sh/claim/tiger73azqrk`) does the same in a browser, for a teammate without a terminal: they sign in, or continue with Google or GitHub to make an account, and accept.

A code works once and expires after 7 days. `surge orgs` lists every org you're in with its members and their roles.

## Publishing as the team

Put the org in front of a new domain the first time it's published:

```sh
surge ./dist acme:docs.acme.com
```

The domain is acme's from then on, and any member publishes it the usual way—no prefix needed:

```sh
surge ./dist docs.acme.com
```

## Bringing in domains you already have

```sh
surge docs.acme.com transfer acme
```

Serving doesn't change: same content, revisions, certificate and DNS. What changes is who can publish and tear the domain down. See [Moving a domain](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#moving-a-domain).

## Private domains

A [private domain](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config#private-domains) the org owns admits every member, and `collaborators` in an [`AUTH` file](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth) means the same people. Someone joining or leaving takes effect straight away, with no republish.

## CI

Give CI a token that belongs to the org, as `SURGE_TOKEN`:

```sh
surge orgs acme tokens add -m "ci"
```

It publishes as acme: the org's domains, and new domains become acme's. It keeps working when the person who added it leaves or resets their password. See [Org tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#tokens) and [Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation).

## When someone leaves

```sh
surge orgs acme members jane@example.com revoke   # remove a member
surge orgs acme leave                             # or leave yourself
```

It takes effect on their next command. The org's domains stay with the org, and so do its tokens: the ones they added keep CI running and are listed when they're removed.

## Plans

Free orgs hold up to three people. An org's domains get Pro's features, such as [`AUTH`](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth), while anyone who can publish them is on [Pro](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/plans).

## Collaborators from before orgs

Before orgs, a domain was shared by inviting people to it one at a time. Those invites are closed. Anyone invited before keeps publishing, and `surge <domain> revoke <email>` removes them.

A team that shared one login gets the same setup: create the org, move the login's domains in, then hand its CI tokens to the org with `surge tokens transfer <id> acme`. Their values don't change, so no pipeline needs touching.

To move a shared domain onto an org:

```sh
surge orgs acme create
surge orgs acme invite                  # a code for each collaborator
surge docs.acme.com transfer acme
surge docs.acme.com revoke jane@example.com   # once jane is a member
```

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs

# Orgs

An org is a named group of accounts. Its **members** are equal: any of them can invite, remove members, and rename the org. Its **admins** are members nobody else can remove or demote. `surge orgs` creates and manages them, and naming an org when you publish a new domain makes the domain the org's: every member can publish it, and it stays with the org when people come and go.

The namespace reads target-first, like the project commands: the org comes first, then the verb.

```sh
surge orgs                                  # every org you belong to, with its members and their roles
surge orgs <org>                            # one org: its name, your role, member count
surge orgs <org> create [--name <name>]     # create it; you become its admin
surge orgs <org> rename <slug> [--name <name>]
surge orgs <org> remove                     # remove the org
```

`<org>` is the org's slug (or its id). Every command that changes something names its org—there's no "current org" to get wrong.

## Creating an org

```sh
surge orgs acme create --name "Acme Inc."
```

The slug (`acme`) is the org's handle; `--name` is the display name and defaults to the slug. Creating an org needs a verified email address (see [`surge verify`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#verify)).

`rename` changes the slug, the name, or both. After a slug change the old slug keeps resolving to the org for 30 days, so scripts and links don't break overnight.

## Members

```sh
surge orgs acme members                            # members and pending invites
surge orgs acme members jane@example.com           # one of them
surge orgs acme members jane@example.com revoke    # remove a member
surge orgs acme members jane@example.com mkadmin   # make an admin
surge orgs acme members jane@example.com rmadmin   # back to member
surge orgs acme leave                              # leave the org yourself
```

Any member can invite and remove members. Making an admin (`mkadmin`, or `invite --admin`), demoting or removing an admin, and removing the org are for admins. Anyone can leave with `surge orgs acme leave`. An org always keeps at least one admin, so the last admin makes someone else an admin before leaving. The last member leaving removes the org, the same as `surge orgs acme remove`—and like `remove`, that waits until the org's domains are transferred or torn down.

### Inviting someone

```sh
surge orgs acme invite            # prints an invite code and its claim link
surge claim tiger73azqrk          # run by whoever you give it to
```

`invite` prints a code like `tiger73azqrk` and a link, `https://auth.surge.sh/claim/tiger73azqrk`, and emails nothing: send one of them to the person yourself. Whoever runs `surge claim` with the code, or opens the link and accepts, joins acme from whichever account they're signed in as. The link works without a terminal: it shows what the code does, signs the person in (Google or GitHub makes them an account if they don't have one), and asks before it accepts. `invite --admin` makes a code that joins as an admin.

A code works once and expires after 7 days. Several can wait at once, up to 10 per org; `surge orgs acme members` lists them by their first word, since the codes themselves aren't kept. To cancel one before it's used:

```sh
surge scrap tiger73azqrk
```

`scrap` cancels a transfer code the same way.

## Publishing to an org

Put the org in front of a new domain:

```sh
surge ./dist acme:docs.acme.com
```

The domain becomes acme's on its first publish, and the result says so: `Published to docs.acme.com (owned by acme)`. From then on any member publishes it with or without the prefix. A domain that already belongs to someone—you included—is never moved by a publish; the prefix only claims domains nobody holds yet. To bring a domain you already own into the org, [transfer it](#moving-a-domain).

An org's domains share the org's publishing limits. Once a day, members get one email listing the new domains the others added and the ones they tore down.

## Tokens

An org token publishes as the org, so CI keeps working whoever comes and goes:

```sh
surge orgs acme tokens                                   # the org's tokens: id, scope, msg, who added it, uses, last used
surge orgs acme tokens add -m "ci"                       # shown once: give it to CI as SURGE_TOKEN
surge orgs acme tokens add --domain '*.previews.acme.com' -m "previews"
surge orgs acme tokens rem tok-1a2b3c4d                  # stops it at once
```

The token belongs to the org, not to whoever added it. It publishes the org's domains, and a new domain it publishes becomes the org's. Someone leaving the org, resetting their password or deleting their account doesn't touch it; only `rem` or removing the org ends it. When a member is removed, the org tokens they added are listed so you can `rem` any you want rotated.

An org token publishes and nothing more: publishing, rollback, cutover, teardown, `list` and `status` on the org's domains. Members, tokens, transfers, settings and DNS need a member signed in as themselves. `--domain` narrows a token to some of the org's domains, or to every name under a pattern like `*.previews.acme.com`. Any member can add and remove the org's tokens, and they're in the daily email too.

Already have a token on a shared login that CI uses? Move the login's domains into the org first, then the token: `surge tokens transfer tok-1a2b3c4d acme`. Its value doesn't change, so nothing in CI needs updating, and from then on it publishes as the org.

## Moving a domain

```sh
surge docs.acme.com transfer acme                # into an org you're in
surge docs.acme.com transfer jane@example.com    # out of the org, to your own account
```

The owner of a domain can move it into any org they belong to. Any member can move an org's domain out to their own account, or into another org they're in. The org's other members get an email as soon as a domain joins or leaves.

Serving is unchanged: the same content, revisions, certificate and DNS. What changes is who can publish and tear the domain down, and whose limits its publishes count against. `surge docs.acme.com status` shows who owns a domain.

### Giving a domain to someone else

```sh
surge docs.acme.com transfer      # prints a transfer code and its claim link
surge claim tiger73azqrk          # run by whoever you give it to
```

`transfer` with nothing after it prints a code like `tiger73azqrk`—a word, two digits and five letters, short enough to read out on a call—and a link to claim it in a browser, `https://auth.surge.sh/claim/tiger73azqrk`. Send either to the person who should have the domain: when they run `surge claim tiger73azqrk` (capitals and spaces don't matter), or open the link and accept, the domain becomes theirs and you no longer reach it. A code works once, expires after 7 days, and stops working if the domain moves some other way first. Making a new code cancels the last one.

In a terminal, `surge claim` shows what a code does before it does it—the domain and who it's from, or the org and the role—and asks. Answer no and the code still works. `--yes` claims without asking, and scripts and agents never get asked.

This is how an agent hands a domain it published to the person it works for. To put a claimed domain in an org, transfer it once it's yours.

## Limits

Free orgs hold up to five people, admins and members together—pending invites don't count until they're accepted, and tokens never do. Each account can be the admin of up to three free orgs. An org can have up to 10 tokens.

## Removing an org

```sh
surge orgs acme remove
```

The slug is free for anyone to use as soon as the org is gone. Removal is refused while the org holds any domains, and the refusal lists them: transfer them out or tear them down first.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account

# Account, Plans & Tokens

Your Surge account is created and managed entirely from the CLI. The account commands take no target—they're about who's typing, not any particular project—so they all sit at the top level.

## login

```sh
surge login
```

Prompts for email and password. If the email has no account yet, **one is created**—login and signup are the same step. On success, a token is stored in your `~/.netrc` file (readable only by you), and every subsequent command uses it silently.

Mistype your password three times and the CLI offers to email you reset instructions.

### Sign in with the browser

```sh
surge login --browser
```

Instead of a password prompt, the CLI prints a link and a four-letter code, opens your browser, and waits. Sign in on the page—with Google, GitHub, or your email and password—check that the code on the screen matches your terminal, and approve. The CLI picks up the token and stores it exactly as a password login would. If a [passkey](#mfa) is on the account, *Use a passkey instead* signs you in with the key alone.

Nothing about the stored session differs between the two: same `~/.netrc` entry, same token, same `surge logout`. It works over SSH too—the link opens on any browser, anywhere. Accounts with [two-factor auth](#mfa) on sign in this way.

## logout

```sh
surge logout
```

Removes the session's token from `~/.netrc` and expires it, so it can never be used again—by you or anything that saw it. Log in again to mint a fresh one.

## whoami

```
$ surge whoami

   you@example.com - Free
   tok-1a2b3c4d · full account
```

Shows the logged-in account and its plan. When the CLI is authenticating with a token (`SURGE_TOKEN` or `--token`), it also prints the token's id and scope—`tok-1a2b3c4d`, scoped to the domains it can publish, or full account—so a pipeline or agent can confirm it holds the least-privilege token it expects without printing the secret. When the credentials don't work, `whoami` says so and exits `1`.

## verify

```sh
surge verify
```

Sends a verification link to your account's email address. Verifying matters:

- **Serving.** A newly signed-up account's `surge.sh` domains serve for their first 90 minutes. After that they report **ready**—published, and serving once you verify your email—until the address is verified. Verify and they serve again; nothing to republish.
- **Rate limits.** Unverified accounts publish under half the usual [limits](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#publishing-limits).

Already verified? The command says so and sends nothing.

## mfa

```sh
surge mfa
```

Two-factor auth for your account. The command opens a page in your browser and gets out of the way—setup and management both happen there, so no secret, code, or recovery code ever passes through a terminal.

Turning it on: sign in fresh on the page and add a factor.

- **A passkey**—a hardware key, Touch ID, Windows Hello, or a passkey your browser or password manager keeps. Every key needs its PIN or biometric; a ceremony that skips that step is refused. Add as many keys as you like, each with a name, and remove them one at a time.
- **An authenticator app**—add the key the page shows to your app and confirm with a code.

The first factor you add mints ten recovery codes—each signs you in once if you lose every factor, and they're shown exactly once. Save them.

With two-factor on:

- Your password alone signs nothing in. `surge login` points you at `surge login --browser`. On the sign-in page, *Use a passkey instead* signs you in with the key alone—no password involved—or sign in with your password and answer with a code from your app. Google and GitHub sign-in carry their own second factor and work as before.
- **Tokens are untouched.** CI, scripts, and agents holding a token keep working—two-factor guards the ceremonies that create credentials, never the credentials themselves.
- Adding or removing keys, and turning two-factor off, happen on the same page (`surge mfa` again) and require a current code or a recovery code. Removing your last factor turns two-factor off.

## tokens

A token lets anything that isn't you—a CI pipeline, a script, an agent—publish as your account. Mint one per use, label it, and scope it to just the domain it needs:

```sh
surge tokens list                              # every token: id, scope, msg, uses, last used
surge tokens add [--domain <domain>] [-m <msg>]  # mint a token
surge tokens rem <id>                          # expire a token
surge tokens transfer <id> <org>               # hand a token to an org, value unchanged
```

```
$ surge tokens add --domain lucid-example.surge.sh -m "github actions"

   f3a1c98c42d76c1ba9d3a9f4e3c0ffee

   Scoped to lucid-example.surge.sh — github actions
```

The token itself is shown once, at mint time—copy it then. Everywhere else it's represented by its id (`tok-1a2b3c4d`), which is what `tokens list` shows and `tokens rem` takes. The `-m` message is how you remember what a token is for, and the `uses` and `last used` columns tell you whether it's still earning its keep.

A token minted with `--domain` is scoped: it can publish to that domain and run its project commands (revisions, config, stats, teardown), and nothing else—no DNS records, collaborators, certificate changes, or billing, and no other domain. Repeat the flag to scope one token to several domains (`--domain a.example.com --domain b.example.com`), or scope it to a pattern (`--domain '*.previews.example.com'`) to cover every name under it—handy for a preview per branch. Without `--domain`, the token has full account access.

A token for a team's pipeline belongs on the [org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#tokens), where it keeps working whoever leaves. `tokens transfer` moves one of yours there without changing its value.

See [CI & Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation) for putting tokens to work.

## plan

```sh
surge plan
```

Shows the available plans—**Free** and **Pro**—with pricing and perks, and lets you switch with an interactive picker—upgrade or downgrade at any time. Card entry happens inline the first time Pro needs one. What each plan includes is on [Plans](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/plans).

Prefer the browser for anything billing-related:

```sh
surge plan --web       # upgrade via browser checkout
surge plan --manage    # manage plan, card & invoices in the browser
```

Both print a private link (valid 48 hours) that opens a secure billing page.

## card

```sh
surge card
```

Updates the payment card on file.

## nuke

```sh
surge nuke
```

**Permanently deletes your account.** There is no undo.

Before you run it:

- **Remove every project.** `surge list` shows what you have. [Tear each one down](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions#tearing-down-a-project) or [give it to someone else](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#giving-a-domain-to-someone-else); the command refuses while any remain.
- **Hand off any org you run.** An org always keeps an admin, so if you are an org's only admin, [make someone else an admin](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#members) or [remove the org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#removing-an-org) first. Any other org you belong to, you leave automatically.

Deleting removes:

- **Your account**—its email address and password.
- **Your plan.** A paid plan is cancelled and the saved card is removed, so nothing is charged again.
- **Your tokens.** Every token on the account stops working at once. Tokens you added to an org belong to the org and keep working until an org admin removes them.
- **Your sign-in** on the machine you ran it from.

The email address is free afterward; signing up with it again starts a new, empty account.
