Can't sign in? Mistype your password three times and the CLI offers to email you reset instructions. If you no longer have the account's email address, write to support@surge.sh.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation

# CI & Automation

Everything the CLI does interactively it also does non-interactively: pass the project and domain as arguments, supply a token instead of logging in, and `surge` runs prompt-free in any pipeline.

## Mint a token

On your own machine, where you're logged in:

```sh
surge tokens add --domain example.com -m "ci"
```

Copy the token it prints into your CI provider's secret store as `SURGE_TOKEN`. The CLI picks that environment variable up automatically—no login step in the pipeline:

```sh
SURGE_TOKEN=… surge ./dist example.com
```

A `--token <token>` flag is also accepted where an environment variable is awkward.

Tokens never face a two-factor challenge: turning [two-factor auth](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#mfa) on for your account guards the ceremonies that create credentials, and leaves every pipeline holding a token running untouched.

Scoping the token with `--domain` means a leaked CI secret can publish to that one domain and nothing else; the `-m` message is how you'll recognize it later. Rotate or kill a pipeline's access any time with `surge tokens rem <id>`—see [tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#tokens).

For a team, add the token to the [org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#tokens) instead: `surge orgs acme tokens add -m "ci"`. It publishes as the org, so the pipeline doesn't stop when the person who set it up leaves or resets their password.

## The non-interactive rule

`surge` only prompts for information it doesn't have. Give it everything up front and it never asks:

```sh
surge ./dist example.com          # path + domain as arguments…
surge ./dist publish              # …or the CNAME file a previous publish wrote
```

If a required value is missing *and* there's no terminal to ask on, the command aborts rather than hangs—so a misconfigured pipeline fails fast. With no token and no stored login, that's:

```txt
Aborted - not logged in and no terminal to ask. Run `surge login` in a terminal, or set SURGE_TOKEN.
```

printed to stderr, with exit code `1`. An unset or misspelled `SURGE_TOKEN` fails the job instead of passing it.

To check what a pipeline is running as before it acts, run `surge whoami`: with a token it prints the token's id and scope, and it exits `1` when the credentials don't work.

## Behind a proxy

The CLI honors the standard proxy variables—`HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY` (or their lowercase spellings)—and `NO_PROXY` for hosts that should bypass it. Nothing else to configure.

## npm scripts

Make publishing part of the project by installing surge as a dev dependency:

```sh
npm install --save-dev surge
```

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build",
    "deploy": "npm run build && surge ./dist example.com"
  }
}
```

Now `npm run deploy` works for everyone on the team (each using their own account, through an [org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams)), and in CI with `SURGE_TOKEN` set.

## GitHub Actions and other CI

[Publish from GitHub Actions](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/github-actions) has the complete workflow—a preview for every pull request, production on every merge. The same shape works in GitLab CI, CircleCI, or any runner with Node available: build, then `surge <path> <domain>` with `SURGE_TOKEN` in the environment.

Scheduled jobs and loops should keep each domain under 200 publishes a day: publish every 10 minutes or less often, or only when the build output changed. See [publishing limits](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#publishing-limits).

## Previews per branch

The [preview flow](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews) maps naturally onto pull requests—publish every branch build as a preview, and cut over on merge:

```sh
# on pull request builds
surge ./dist example.com --preview -m "$COMMIT_MESSAGE"

# on merge to main
surge ./dist example.com
```

Each PR build gets a stable revision URL to link in the review, and production only moves when main does.

## Git hooks

For a lighter-weight setup—no CI service at all—publish from a local git hook. Git has no hook that runs after a push, so use `pre-push`, which runs on every `git push` (a failed publish stops the push):

```sh
printf '#!/bin/sh\nsurge ./dist example.com\n' > .git/hooks/pre-push
chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-push
```

Or use `husky`/`simple-git-hooks` to version the hook with the project.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/what-surge-sends

# What Surge Sends

A publish sends your project and the details the platform needs to put it online. This page lists all of it, so you can check it against the source and against your own network traffic.

## With every publish

- **Your project's files**, packed as a gzipped tarball under the project folder's name. For projects over 1 MB, files the domain already has are [left out](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing).
- **Your credential**: the token from `surge login`, `SURGE_TOKEN`, or `--token`.
- **The domain** you're publishing to.
- **The file count and total size** of the project.
- **The arguments you passed**, as you typed them, so the platform can act on flags like `--preview`, `-m` and `--private`. A project path typed in full, like `/Users/you/site/dist`, travels as typed.
- **The CLI's version**, its command name (`surge`, or the tool embedding it), and the time the publish started.
- **A User-Agent** saying how the CLI was called (below).

Like any request, a publish also reaches us from your IP address.

## The User-Agent

```txt
surge/0.54.0 (auth=env; ci=0; tty=0; via=npx; agent=claude-code)
```

| Field | Values | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `auth` | `netrc`, `env`, `flag` | Where the credential came from: the saved login, `SURGE_TOKEN`, or `--token` |
| `ci` | `0`, `1` | Whether the `CI` environment variable is set |
| `tty` | `0`, `1` | Whether a terminal is attached |
| `via` | `npx`, `installed` | Whether the CLI ran through `npx` or from an installed copy |
| `agent` | a name, or absent | The AI agent running the CLI, when it identifies itself |

`agent` comes from the `AI_AGENT` environment variable (only the name before any `_`, `/` or `@`, so `claude-code_2-1-300_agent` is sent as `claude-code`). Without it, the CLI looks for a few variables agents set in the shells they run: `CLAUDECODE`, `CURSOR_AGENT`, `GEMINI_CLI`, `CODEX_SANDBOX`, `REPL_ID` and `E2B_SANDBOX`. It checks whether they're set, and never sends what they contain.

We use it to see how Surge is used—by people at a terminal, by CI, and by agents—so we can make each of them work well.

## Never sent

- The value of any environment variable
- Your hostname or operating system
- Any file outside the project you're publishing
- Anything about other software on your machine, beyond the agent name above

The User-Agent's fields are names and `0`/`1` only. A change to what the CLI sends will be listed in the release notes and on this page.

See the [Privacy Policy](https://surge.sh/privacy) for how Surge handles what it receives.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/cli/reference

# Command Reference

The complete `surge` command surface. Run `surge --help` for the built-in overview, and `surge <command> --help` for one command's usage.

Project commands are written here as `surge <domain> <verb>`, but the target slot takes three forms: a **domain**, a **path** to a project directory, or nothing at all—in which case the current directory's project is the target. `surge example.com rollback`, `surge ./dist rollback`, and `surge rollback` are the same command. Account commands take no target.

Commands typed in the older, verb-first order (`surge rollback example.com`) keep working forever, silently—both orders are first-class. A few commands don't appear on the `--help` overview—`zone`, `token`—power tools it doesn't spend lines on; this page documents everything. `surge account <verb>` also dispatches to the flat identity commands (`surge account whoami` = `surge whoami`).

## Global flags

| Flag | Alias | Description |
|------|-------|-------------|
| `--project <path>` | `-p` | The directory to publish. Also settable as the first positional argument. |
| `--domain <domain>` | `-d` | The domain to act on. Also settable as a positional argument or via the `CNAME` file. |
| `--preview` | `--stage`, `-s` | Publish a [preview](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews) instead of cutting over production. |
| `--message <msg>` | `-m` | Attach a [message](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#messages) to the revision (or to a token at `tokens add`). |
| `--force <protocol>` | | `https` (or `http`) redirects all traffic to that protocol. Sticks as [configuration](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config). |
| `--private` / `--public` | | Lock the domain to the people who can publish it, or open it again. See [private domains](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config#private-domains). |
| `--token <token>` | | Authenticate with a token instead of the stored login. The `SURGE_TOKEN` environment variable does the same. |
| `--endpoint <url>` | `-e` | Target a different Surge API endpoint. |
| `--version` | `-V` | Print the CLI version. |
| `--help` | `-h` | Print the command listing, adapted to the target—or one command's usage after a verb. |

Publish-intent flags carry their own routing: `surge ./dist -d example.com` and bare `surge --preview` are publishes, no verb needed.

## Environment

| Variable | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `SURGE_TOKEN` | A [token](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#tokens) to authenticate with—no login, no prompt. `--token` wins when both are set. |
| `HTTPS_PROXY` / `HTTP_PROXY` / `ALL_PROXY` | Send API traffic through a proxy (lowercase spellings work too). |
| `NO_PROXY` | Hosts that bypass the proxy. |

With no stored login, no token, and no terminal to prompt on, a command that needs an account aborts on stderr—`` Aborted - not logged in and no terminal to ask. Run `surge login` in a terminal, or set SURGE_TOKEN. ``—and exits `1`. See [CI & Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation#the-non-interactive-rule).

## Publishing

### `surge <path> <domain>`

Publish a directory to a domain—or a single HTML file, published as the domain's [`index.html`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#a-single-html-file). Pass `_` as the domain for a freshly generated `.surge.sh` subdomain, no prompt. Pass `--force https` to redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS; the setting sticks across publishes. Respects [`.surgeignore`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#ignoring-files). → [Publishing](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing)

### `surge [path] publish`

Publish using the project's own domain—from its [`CNAME` file](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#the-cname-file) when present, prompting with a generated suggestion otherwise (enter `_` at the prompt for a fresh one). This is the everyday form once a project knows where it lives. `deploy` is accepted as a silent alias.

### `surge <domain> teardown`

Remove the project from the domain and the CDN. → [Revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions#tearing-down-a-project)

## Revisions

Surge keeps the last 100 revisions of each domain.

### `surge list [--all] [<org>:]`

Your domains and your orgs' domains, newest publish first: owner (an email or an org), age, last publisher, and on a wide terminal file count and size. Shows the newest 50; `--all` shows every one. `surge list acme:` shows only the domains the org `acme` owns.

### `surge <domain> revs`

The project's revisions—preview URL, age, author, size, and message—with the live revision highlighted. `surge <domain> list` is the same command. → [Revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions)

### `surge <domain> rollback`

Serve the previous revision.

### `surge <domain> rollfore`

Serve the next revision (the inverse of `rollback`).

### `surge <domain> cutover [revision]`

Serve the given revision, or the latest one when omitted. Ships [previews](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews).

### `surge <domain> discard [revision]`

Remove a revision from the system. If it was live, production moves to a neighboring revision; discarding the last revision takes the project offline.

## Domains & DNS

### `surge <domain> dns list`

List the domain's custom DNS records. Bare `dns` prints the available subcommands and Surge's name servers. → [Domains & DNS](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/domains)

### `surge <domain> dns add <type> <name> <value>`

Add a DNS record. MX records take a priority: `dns add MX <priority> <value>` (host defaults to `@`) or `dns add MX <name> <priority> <value>`.

### `surge <domain> dns rem <id>`

Remove a DNS record by the id shown in the listing.

### `surge <domain> zone`

Print the domain's complete zone in BIND format, including records Surge manages automatically. Supports the same `add`/`rem` subcommands as `dns`.

## Debug

### `surge <domain> debug status`

The domain's state: **waiting on dns** (with the records to add), **securing**, **ready** (published, serving once the account's email is verified), or **live**. `surge <domain> status` is the same command. → [Analytics & Diagnostics](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics#status)

### `surge <domain> debug files`

List every file in the live revision with its size, as served by the CDN.

### `surge <domain> debug audit`

Report each edge node's state for the domain: revision, file count, size, certificate validity.

### `surge <domain> debug bust`

Purge the project from the cache on all edge nodes.

### `surge <domain> debug certs`

Show the certificates installed for the domain: subject, issuer, alt names, expiry, auto-renewal. → [SSL Certificates](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/ssl)

### `surge <domain> debug encrypt`

Provision the domain's managed SSL certificate manually. Certificates normally provision and renew automatically.

## Stats

### `surge <domain> stats traffic`

Visits, uniques, connections, encryption share, cache hit rates, top pages, 404s, redirects, and sources for the past two weeks. → [Analytics & Diagnostics](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics)

### `surge <domain> stats audience`

Browsers, operating systems, and devices of your visitors.

### `surge <domain> stats usage`

Per-file bandwidth served, with a projected monthly total.

### `surge <domain> stats load`

Connection volume per datacenter across the network.

## Configuration

### `surge <domain> config`

View the project's platform settings; pass flags to change them: `--force http|https`, `--redirect <domain>`, `--cors <domain>|*`, `--hsts <seconds>`, `--private` / `--public`, any value `null` to clear. Changes apply across the edge immediately. → [Project Configuration](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config)

## Collaborators

Orgs are how people share domains. Collaborator invites are closed. → [Teams](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams#collaborators-from-before-orgs)

### `surge <domain> revoke <emails…>`

Remove a collaborator invited before orgs, immediately.

## Orgs

### `surge orgs`

Every org you belong to, each with its members, their roles and pending invites. `surge orgs <org>` shows one. → [Orgs](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs)

### `surge orgs <org> create [--name <name>]`

Create an org with the slug `<org>`; you become its admin. Needs a verified email.

### `surge orgs <org> rename <slug> [--name <name>]`

Change the slug, the display name, or both. The old slug keeps resolving for 30 days.

### `surge orgs <org> remove`

Remove the org. Refused while it holds any domains: transfer or tear them down first.

### `surge orgs <org> invite [--admin]`

Print a one-time invite code to send to someone yourself; nothing is emailed. `--admin` invites an admin. → [Inviting someone](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#inviting-someone)

### `surge orgs <org> leave`

Leave the org. The last admin can't leave until someone else is an admin; the last member leaving removes the org, as `remove` does. → [Members](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#members)

### `surge orgs <org> members [<email> [revoke|mkadmin|rmadmin]]`

List members and pending invites, show one, remove a member, or change a role. Members are equal, except that only admins make, demote or remove an admin. → [Orgs](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs)

### `surge orgs <org> tokens [add [--domain <domain>] [-m <msg>] | rem <id>]`

List, add or remove the org's tokens. An org token publishes as the org and keeps working whoever leaves; any member manages them. → [Org tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#tokens)

### `surge <path> <org>:<domain>`

Publish a new domain owned by the org; any member can. → [Publishing to an org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#publishing-to-an-org)

### `surge <domain> transfer [<org> | <your email>]`

Move the domain into an org you're in, or out to your own account. With nothing after it, print a transfer code for giving the domain to someone else. Serving is unchanged. → [Moving a domain](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#moving-a-domain)

### `surge claim <code> [--yes]`

Join the org an invite code is for, or take the domain a transfer code names into your account. In a terminal it shows what the code does and asks first; `--yes` doesn't ask. In a browser, `https://auth.surge.sh/claim/<code>` does the same.

### `surge scrap <code>`

Cancel an invite or transfer code. It stops working at once.

## Account

### `surge login`

Authenticate (or create an account) and store a token in `~/.netrc`. → [Account, Plans & Tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account)

### `surge logout`

Remove the stored token and expire it.

### `surge whoami`

Show the logged-in email and plan—or, when authenticating with a token, the token's id and scope. Exits `1` when not authenticated.

### `surge verify`

Send an email verification link to your address.

### `surge login --browser`

Sign in via the browser—any provider, approve with a code match. → [Account, Plans & Tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#sign-in-with-the-browser)

### `surge mfa`

Open the browser page that sets up or manages two-factor auth—passkeys and authenticator apps. → [Account, Plans & Tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#mfa)

### `surge tokens list`

Every token on the account: id, scope, message, uses, created, last used. → [Tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#tokens)

### `surge tokens add [--domain <domain>] [-m <msg>]`

Mint a token—shown once, at mint time. `--domain` scopes it to one domain or a pattern like `*.previews.example.com` (repeat the flag for several); `-m` labels it.

### `surge tokens rem <id>`

Expire a token by its `tok-` id.

### `surge tokens transfer <id> <org>`

Hand one of your tokens to an org you're in. Its value doesn't change; from then on it publishes as the org. → [Org tokens](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#tokens)

### `surge token`

Print the token the CLI is currently authenticating with.

### `surge plan [--web | --manage]`

Change your account plan interactively, or print a private browser link for checkout (`--web`) or full billing management (`--manage`).

### `surge card`

Update the payment card on file.

### `surge nuke`

Permanently delete your account. Refuses while any project remains or while you are an org's only admin. See [Account](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#nuke) for what it removes.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/

# Guides

The [CLI docs](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/) explain every command and the [Platform docs](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/) explain how serving works. Guides are the third thing: complete walkthroughs of the task you actually showed up with, start to finish, with nothing assumed and nothing left dangling.

Every guide ends the same way, because every path through Surge ends the same way: your project propagated to [every edge node of the CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) before the command finishes—live everywhere, instantly, with an undo.

## Publish your framework's build

Any tool that produces a directory of static files works with Surge—these cover the details that differ, like where the `CNAME` file belongs so it survives your build:

- [Publish a Vite Project](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/vite)
- [Publish an Astro Project](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/astro)
- [Publish an Eleventy Project](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/eleventy)
- [Publish a Single-Page App](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/spa) — React Router, Vue Router, or any client-side routing

## Automate

- [Publish from GitHub Actions](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/github-actions) — a preview per pull request, production on merge

## Domains

- [Put a Project on Your Own Domain](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/custom-domain) — registrar to `live`, the whole path

## Migrate

- [Migrate from GitHub Pages](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/github-pages)
- [Migrate from Netlify](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/netlify)

Using a tool that isn't covered? The recipe is always the same shape: build, then `surge <output-directory> <domain>`. If your tool makes a folder of files, you're already done—[Getting Started](https://surge.sh/docs/getting-started) is the generic version.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/vite

# Publish a Vite Project

Vite builds to a `dist/` directory of plain static files—exactly what Surge publishes. Total time from a fresh project to live on the web: about two minutes, most of it npm.

## Build and publish

```sh
npm create vite@latest my-project
cd my-project
npm install
npm run build
surge ./dist my-project.surge.sh
```

That's the entire flow. The publish output confirms your project propagating to every node of [Surge's CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn)—when it prints `Success!`, you're live worldwide:

```
$ surge ./dist lucid-example.surge.sh

   Running as you@example.com (Free)

        project: ./dist
         domain: lucid-example.surge.sh
           size: 3 files, 672 bytes
         upload: [=========================] 100%
            CDN: [=========================] 100%
     encryption: [=========================] 100%

  ┌──────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │   CERT   │   *.surge.sh, surge.sh                                         │   auto-renew          │
  ├──────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │   DNS    │   using Surge Name Servers                                     │   geo-aware           │
  └──────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘
  ┌──────────┬──────────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────┬─────────┐
  │   HTTP   │   sfo.surge.sh   │   US, San Francisco   │   138.197.235.123   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   lhr.surge.sh   │   GB, London          │   46.101.67.123     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   yyz.surge.sh   │   CA, Toronto         │   159.203.50.177    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   jfk.surge.sh   │   US, New York        │   159.203.159.100   │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   ams.surge.sh   │   NL, Amsterdam       │   188.166.132.94    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   fra.surge.sh   │   DE, Frankfurt       │   138.68.112.220    │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   sgp.surge.sh   │   SG, Singapore       │   139.59.195.30     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   blr.surge.sh   │   IN, Bangalore       │   139.59.50.135     │   D.Ocean   │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   syd.surge.sh   │   AU, Sydney          │   45.76.126.95      │   Vultr     │   ✔ ◍   │
  │   HTTP   │   nrt.surge.sh   │   JP, Tokyo           │   172.104.96.133    │   Linode    │   ✔ ◍   │
  └──────────┴──────────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────┴─────────┘
   Live preview ................................................ 1785787164375--lucid-example.surge.sh
   Latest ............................................................. latest--lucid-example.surge.sh
   Production ................................................................. lucid-example.surge.sh

   Success! - Published to lucid-example.surge.sh

   domain written to dist/CNAME
```

## Keep the domain across builds

That first publish wrote the domain to `dist/CNAME`—but `vite build` wipes and recreates `dist/`, so the next build would lose it. Move it to `public/`, which Vite copies verbatim into every build:

```sh
mv dist/CNAME public/CNAME
```

Now the domain travels with every build, and publishing needs no arguments:

```sh
npm run build && surge ./dist publish
```

## Make it a script

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build",
    "deploy": "vite build && surge ./dist publish"
  }
}
```

`npm run deploy` now builds and publishes in one move—for you, for teammates in your [org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams), and for [CI](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/github-actions).

## If you're using a router

Vite + React Router (or Vue Router, or any client-side routing with real URLs) needs one extra file so deep links survive refresh—see [Publish a Single-Page App](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/spa).

## Custom domain

Publish to your own domain the same way—`surge ./dist example.com`—and the output walks you through pointing DNS. The full path is in [Put a Project on Your Own Domain](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/custom-domain).

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/astro

# Publish an Astro Project

Astro is static-first: `astro build` emits a `dist/` directory of finished HTML, and Surge puts directories of finished HTML on the web. The two need no adapter, no configuration, and no server.

## Build and publish

```sh
npm create astro@latest my-project
cd my-project
npm run build
surge ./dist my-project.surge.sh
```

The publish propagates to [every edge node](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) while the command runs—`Success!` means live in every region, not queued for it.

## Keep the domain across builds

That first publish wrote the domain to `dist/CNAME`—but the next `astro build` recreates `dist/` and would lose it. Astro copies everything in `public/` straight into the build, so that's the file's home:

```sh
mv dist/CNAME public/CNAME
```

Every subsequent build carries its domain, and `surge ./dist publish` needs no arguments. Wire it into your scripts:

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "astro build",
    "deploy": "astro build && surge ./dist publish"
  }
}
```

## The 404 page

Add `src/pages/404.astro` and Astro emits `404.html`—which is exactly the file [Surge serves for missing paths](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-404). Style your not-found page like any other page of the project; nothing to configure on the platform side.

## View transitions, islands, and client JS

All of Astro's client-side behavior ships as static assets, so it publishes like everything else. The one Astro feature Surge doesn't run is SSR (`output: 'server'`)—Surge serves files, it doesn't execute them. Astro's default static output is the fit.

## Custom domain

`surge ./dist example.com` and follow the DNS records the output prints—[the full walkthrough](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/custom-domain) covers delegation, certificates, and forcing HTTPS.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/eleventy

# Publish an Eleventy Project

Eleventy renders to `_site/` by default, and a rendered `_site/` is a finished Surge project. No plugin, no adapter.

## Build and publish

```sh
npx @11ty/eleventy
surge ./_site my-project.surge.sh
```

The publish output confirms every node of [the CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) individually—your project is live worldwide when the command returns, not minutes later.

## Keep the domain across builds

That first publish wrote the domain to `_site/CNAME`—but Eleventy rebuilds `_site/`, so move the file to the project root and tell Eleventy to pass it through to every build:

```sh
mv _site/CNAME CNAME
```

```js
// eleventy.config.js
export default function (eleventyConfig) {
  eleventyConfig.addPassthroughCopy("CNAME")
}
```

Now every build lands in `_site/` with its domain aboard, and publishing is argument-free:

```sh
npx @11ty/eleventy && surge ./_site publish
```

## Ignore the sources

If you publish from the project root instead of `_site/` by accident, [`.surgeignore`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#ignoring-files) is the guard rail—but the cleaner habit is what this guide shows: publish the output directory, keep sources out of the question entirely.

## Custom domain

Same command, your domain: `surge ./_site example.com`. The output prints the DNS records to add, and [the custom-domain guide](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/custom-domain) walks the whole path to `live`.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/spa

# Publish a Single-Page App

A single-page app with client-side routing—React Router, Vue Router, SvelteKit's static adapter, anything with real URLs—has one hosting requirement: when a visitor lands directly on `/dashboard/settings`, the server must hand them the app shell instead of a 404, and let the router take it from there.

On Surge, that behavior is a file name.

## The 200.html file

Name your app shell `200.html` (or ship a copy of `index.html` under that name) and [Surge serves it for every path that doesn't match a real file](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/spa-routing)—with a `200` status, at the URL the visitor asked for. The router boots, reads the address bar, and renders the right view. Deep links work. Refresh works. Shared links work.

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build && cp dist/index.html dist/200.html",
    "deploy": "npm run build && surge ./dist publish"
  }
}
```

That `cp` is the entire integration. Works identically for any bundler—the only requirement is that the output directory ends up containing `200.html`.

## Why 200 and not 404 tricks

Some hosts fake SPA routing by serving the shell from the 404 page. That answers deep links with a `404` status—search engines and monitoring see errors on every route. Surge's `200.html` answers with `200`, because your routes aren't errors. Keep [`404.html`](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-404) for what it's for: paths your app genuinely doesn't know.

## Publish it

```sh
npm run deploy
```

The whole app—shell, assets, both special files—propagates to [every edge node](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) during the publish. Every route of your app is served from the node nearest each visitor, because every route *is* the shell, and the shell is everywhere.

Your first publish writes the domain to a `CNAME` file in the output directory; move it to wherever your bundler copies static files verbatim (`public/` for Vite and Astro) so it survives rebuilds—details in the [Vite guide](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/vite).

## Hash routing needs nothing

If your router uses `#` URLs, every path is really `/`, and plain `index.html` already handles it. `200.html` is for routers using the History API—which is what you want anyway, and now it costs one file copy.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/github-actions

# Publish from GitHub Actions

The goal: every pull request gets a preview URL, and merging to `main` publishes production. One workflow file, one secret, and the [preview machinery](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews) does the rest—production never moves until main does.

## 1. Mint a scoped token

On your own machine, where you're logged in:

```sh
surge tokens add --domain example.com -m "github actions"
```

The token prints once—copy it into your repository's secrets as `SURGE_TOKEN` (*Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions*). Because it's scoped with `--domain`, a leaked secret can publish to this one domain and do nothing else; the `-m` message is how you'll recognize it in [`surge tokens list`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#tokens), and `surge tokens rem` is the kill switch that rotates it.

If the domain belongs to an [org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams), add the token to the org instead, so the workflow keeps running when whoever set it up leaves: `surge orgs acme tokens add --domain example.com -m "github actions"`.

## 2. The workflow

```yaml
name: Publish
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm ci && npm run build

      # pull requests from this repo: upload a preview - production untouched
      - if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
        run: npx surge ./dist example.com --preview
        env:
          SURGE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SURGE_TOKEN }}

      # merges to main: publish production
      - if: github.event_name == 'push'
        run: npx surge ./dist example.com
        env:
          SURGE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SURGE_TOKEN }}
```

The preview step's log ends with the revision's own URL—`Preview available at …`, a host like `1785787164375--example--com.surge.sh` for a custom domain, and `latest--example--com.surge.sh` always shows the newest—a complete copy of the built app on the same CDN production uses, safe to link in the PR discussion and point tests at. The production step is a full publish: propagated to [every edge node](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) before the job goes green, so a green check means *live*, not *queued*.

## Notes worth knowing

- **`SURGE_TOKEN` is picked up from the environment automatically**—no login step, no config file. The CLI [never prompts when it has what it needs](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation#the-non-interactive-rule), and aborts rather than hangs if something's missing, so a misconfigured pipeline fails fast and loud.
- **Fork pull requests don't receive secrets** on GitHub, which is why the preview step only runs for same-repo branches: without it, a fork's build would reach `surge` with an empty `SURGE_TOKEN` and fail the job. That's GitHub's security model, and for a token that can publish to your domain, it's the behavior you want.
- **Rollback is your incident response.** A bad merge that went live is one `surge example.com rollback` from gone—instant and global, from any machine you're logged into. No revert-commit-and-wait-for-CI required (though the revert can follow at leisure).

The same shape works in GitLab CI, CircleCI, or any runner with Node: build, then `surge <dir> <domain>` with `SURGE_TOKEN` set. More patterns in [CI & Automation](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/automation).

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/custom-domain

# Put a Project on Your Own Domain

Custom domains are free on Surge, certificates included and provisioned for you. This is the whole path: from a domain at a registrar to `live`, with the platform telling you whose move it is at every step.

## 1. Publish to the domain

Don't wait for DNS—publish first:

```sh
surge ./dist example.com
```

The publish succeeds immediately (your files are on [the CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn), staged), and the output reports the domain as **waiting on dns** along with the exact records to add. That status is the platform's honest answer to "why isn't it up yet?"—and it's the only step that's ever yours.

## 2. Point the domain at Surge

Pick one of the three ways in—[compared in depth on Custom Domains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains):

```txt
Name servers   ns1.surge.world  ns2.surge.world  ns3.surge.world  ns4.surge.world
CNAME          geo.surge.world
A              138.197.235.123
```

Delegating to the name servers is recommended: geo-aware routing, the apex and every subdomain covered, and extra records managed [from the CLI](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/domains). Recreate any records the domain already depends on before you switch. Keeping DNS at your current provider? Use a `CNAME` for subdomains, and an `A` record (or your provider's ALIAS/ANAME) for the apex.

## 3. Watch it go live

```sh
surge example.com status
```

The domain moves through three states, and only the first is yours: **waiting on dns** (add the records above) → **securing** (DNS is right; Surge is provisioning the certificate—no action, no charge) → **live** (verified by real requests against the actual edge, not a dashboard's optimism). DNS propagation at your registrar is the only wait in the pipeline; Surge picks the domain up the moment the records are in place.

## 4. Force HTTPS

Once live, publish with `--force https` to redirect all plain-HTTP traffic permanently:

```sh
surge ./dist example.com --force https
```

The choice sticks as [project configuration](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config). To have browsers insist on HTTPS too, set an HSTS max-age: `surge example.com config --hsts 31536000`. More in [SSL & HTTPS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl#forcing-https).

## What you get

`www` folds into the apex automatically (or vice versa—whichever you publish is canonical). Every subdomain of a delegated domain is publishable as its own independent project—`surge ./docs docs.example.com`—each with its own [revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) and settings. And the certificate renews itself forever; there is no step 5.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/github-pages

# Migrate from GitHub Pages

Surge and GitHub Pages share the `CNAME` convention—the file in your repo that names your custom domain means the same thing to both. Most projects migrate in minutes, and because both hosts keep serving until DNS moves, there's no downtime window.

## 1. Publish what you already have

Find the directory Pages serves—the repo root, `/docs`, or your build output—and publish it to a test domain first:

```sh
surge ./docs my-project.surge.sh
```

If Pages was building Jekyll for you, build locally and publish the result:

```sh
bundle exec jekyll build
surge ./_site my-project.surge.sh
```

Check the `.surge.sh` URL. That's your project on [Surge's CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn)—already propagated to every region, before you've touched DNS.

## 2. Publish to your real domain

Your repo's existing `CNAME` file already names it, so:

```sh
surge ./docs publish
```

reads the domain straight from the file. The output reports **waiting on dns** with the records to add—your project is staged on the edge, waiting for the domain to arrive.

## 3. Move DNS

At your DNS provider, replace the Pages records (the `185.199.108–111.x` A records, or the `CNAME` to `username.github.io`) with Surge's—either [delegate to Surge's name servers or CNAME to the edge](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/custom-domain#2-point-the-domain-at-surge). Until propagation completes, visitors reach Pages; after, they reach Surge. Both serve the same content the whole way through—no gap, no rush, no maintenance page.

```sh
surge example.com debug status
```

tells you the moment it's **live**, verified against the actual edge. The certificate provisions itself during **securing**—nothing to configure.

## What you gain

Publishing decouples from pushing: ship from your machine, from [CI](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/github-actions), from anywhere—no waiting on a Pages build, and the repo can stay private without a plan discussion. Every publish is a [revision with instant rollback](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions). [Previews](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews) exist. And your not-found page is just [`404.html`](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-404), same as it was.

One honest boundary: `username.github.io` domains belong to GitHub and can't move—this migration is for projects on custom domains, or projects ready to have one. Custom domains are [free on Surge](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/plans), certificate included.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/guides/netlify

# Migrate from Netlify

If your Netlify project is a static build—and most are—migration is: publish the build output, translate a couple of config files, move DNS when ready. Surge has no build minutes to meter because builds happen wherever you like; the platform's job is serving what you built, [instantly and globally](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn).

## 1. Publish the build output

Your `netlify.toml` (or the Netlify UI) names a publish directory—`dist`, `build`, `_site`. Build locally and publish it to a test domain:

```sh
npm run build
surge ./dist my-project.surge.sh
```

Check it end to end on the `.surge.sh` URL before touching anything else.

## 2. Translate the config

| On Netlify | On Surge |
|------------|----------|
| `_redirects` rules | A [`ROUTER` file](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/redirects): `301 /old /new`, with `:segment` patterns. Pro. |
| `/* /index.html 200` (SPA fallback) | Name your shell [`200.html`](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/spa)—free, one file copy in your build script. |
| Custom headers | [Lucid Caching](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn#lucid-caching) replaces cache-header tuning; HSTS and protocol enforcement live in [`surge config`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config). |
| Password protection | An [`AUTH` file](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth). Pro. |
| Deploy previews | [`surge publish --preview`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/previews)—every revision has its own URL on the production CDN. |
| Build hooks / CI | [GitHub Actions in one workflow file](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/github-actions), or any runner with Node. |

The honest boundary: Surge serves static files and doesn't execute anything. Netlify Functions, form handling, and edge functions need a home of their own (an API host of your choosing)—your static front end calls them cross-origin same as before, with [CORS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cors) if you're hosting the API yourself somewhere that needs it.

## 3. Publish to your real domain

```sh
surge ./dist example.com
```

The output reports **waiting on dns** with the records to add—your content is already on every edge node, staged, waiting for the domain. It also writes the domain to `dist/CNAME`; move that file to wherever your bundler copies static assets from (`public/` for most) so rebuilds keep it, and every publish after this one is just `surge ./dist publish`.

## 4. Move DNS

At your registrar, point the domain at Surge—[delegation recommended](https://surge.sh/docs/guides/custom-domain#2-point-the-domain-at-surge), plain CNAME supported. Netlify serves until propagation completes; Surge serves after; nobody sees a gap. `surge example.com debug status` reports **live** the moment the switchover is real, certificate provisioned and verified.

## Afterward

The loop gets simpler: build anywhere, `surge ./dist publish`, done—propagated to every region before the command exits, with [rollback](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) as your safety net. No build queue between you and production, and no bill that scales with how often you ship.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/

# The Surge Platform

Surge is a web publishing platform built for front-end developers. You hand it a directory of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; it hands you back a live domain on a global CDN. The [CLI](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/) is how you drive it—this section documents what the platform itself does with your project once it's up.

## What every project gets

Publish anything to Surge—free—and it comes with:

- **A global edge network.** Your files propagate to [ten regions worldwide](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn) *during* the publish—every node confirms before the CLI says `Success!`—and visitors are served from the nearest one, with [aggressive-but-correct caching](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn#lucid-caching) applied automatically.
- **[Custom domain support](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains).** Publish to your own domain at no cost, with DNS managed by Surge or by your existing provider.
- **[SSL](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl).** Every `surge.sh` subdomain is HTTPS out of the box; custom domains get free managed certificates, provisioned automatically.
- **[Clean URLs](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/clean-urls).** `/about` serves `about.html`, canonical redirects are handled, and `www` folds into your root domain automatically.
- **[Revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions).** The last 100 publishes are kept, each previewable and instantly restorable.
- **[Client-side routing](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/spa-routing)** for single-page apps, and [custom 404 pages](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-404).
- **Gzip, ETags, and far-future caching**—applied for you, never configured.

## Configuration is files in your project

The platform's conventions follow one idea: your project directory is the configuration. Behavior is controlled by files that publish with your code:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `CNAME` | Sets the project's domain. |
| `.surgeignore` | Excludes files from publishing. |
| `200.html` | Serves your app shell for unmatched URLs ([SPA routing](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/spa-routing)). |
| `404.html` | The not-found page ([custom 404s](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-404)). |
| `ROUTER` | Redirect rules ([redirects](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/redirects)). |
| `AUTH` | [Password protection & protected paths](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth)—a password on the project, or Google sign-in on specific paths. |
| `CORS` | Cross-origin access ([CORS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cors)). |

Because these travel with every publish, each [revision](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) carries its own complete configuration—roll back the code and you roll back the behavior with it. The control files themselves (`ROUTER`, `AUTH`, `CORS`) are never served to visitors.

## Free and Pro

Publishing, custom domains, managed SSL, revisions, CORS, and the CDN are free. Pro adds exactly two things: password protection and protected paths (`AUTH`), and redirects (`ROUTER`). See [Plans](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/plans).

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains

# Custom Domains

```txt
Name servers   ns1.surge.world  ns2.surge.world  ns3.surge.world  ns4.surge.world
CNAME          geo.surge.world
A              138.197.235.123
```

Every project on Surge can live at your own domain, free—certificate included. Once the domain points at Surge, publishing to it is identical to publishing to a subdomain:

```sh
surge ./dist example.com
```

Publish first, point DNS second: the publish succeeds immediately and reports the domain as **waiting on dns** along with the records to add. Pointing DNS at Surge is the only step that's ever yours.

There are three ways to point a domain at Surge. They differ in where DNS is managed and in how visitors are routed:

| | Name servers | `CNAME` record | `A` record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DNS managed | by Surge, from the CLI | at your DNS provider | at your DNS provider |
| Covers | the root and every subdomain | subdomains (the root only with `ALIAS`/`ANAME`) | the root or any subdomain |
| Routing | geo-aware—nearest edge | geo-aware—nearest edge | one fixed region |
| Setup | four `NS` records at the registrar | one record per hostname | one record per hostname |

Delegating to Surge's name servers is the recommended path. A `CNAME` is the right choice when DNS has to stay where it is. An `A` record covers the case a `CNAME` can't: the root domain at a provider without `ALIAS`-style records.

## Option 1: Delegate to Surge's name servers (recommended)

Set your domain's name servers, at your registrar, to:

```txt
ns1.surge.world
ns2.surge.world
ns3.surge.world
ns4.surge.world
```

Surge then answers DNS for the whole domain. The root and every subdomain—including the wildcard that makes [subdomains](#subdomains) publishable—resolve to the edge node nearest each visitor, and there are no individual records to add or maintain for your projects.

Delegation moves *all* of the domain's DNS to Surge, so any records you rely on today—mail, verification strings, subdomains hosted elsewhere—need to be recreated with [the `dns` commands](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/domains). Add them before switching the name servers and nothing skips a beat:

```sh
surge example.com dns add MX 10 mail.example.com
surge example.com dns add TXT @ "v=spf1 include:_spf.example.net ~all"
surge example.com dns add CNAME app app.example.dev
```

Delegated domains also get a single wildcard certificate covering the root and every subdomain—see [SSL & HTTPS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl#custom-domains).

## Option 2: `CNAME` record at your current DNS provider

Keep DNS where it is and point each hostname at Surge's `CNAME` target:

```txt
www      CNAME   geo.surge.world
```

`geo.surge.world` is answered by Surge's name servers, so a `CNAME` is geo-aware too—visitors still resolve to the nearest edge, without geo-answers from your provider. Add one record per hostname you publish to, or a wildcard (`*`) record to make every subdomain publishable at once.

The root domain (`example.com` itself) can't carry a `CNAME`—the DNS specification doesn't allow it. Providers that offer an `ALIAS`, `ANAME`, or "flattened `CNAME`" record type let you point the root at `geo.surge.world` all the same. At a provider without one, use an [`A` record](#option-3-a-record-at-your-current-dns-provider) for the root and a `CNAME` for `www`.

The earlier targets `geo.surge.sh` and `na-west1.surge.sh` keep working and are geo-aware too; there's no need to change a record that already has one.

## Option 3: `A` record at your current DNS provider

Point the hostname directly at a Surge edge address:

```txt
@        A       138.197.235.123
```

This is the address the CLI prints after every publish that's waiting on dns, and it works for the root or any subdomain. The trade-off is routing: an `A` record pins the hostname to a single region, so every visitor is served from that edge rather than the nearest one—the publish output reports it as **using Surge A Record, not geo-aware**. The server table in that same output lists every region's address; any of them works as an `A` record and pins the domain to that region instead.

Two things to keep in mind:

- The hostname must resolve *only* to Surge. Mixing a Surge address with another host's `A` record round-robins visitors between the two, and Surge treats the domain as not pointed.
- The most common arrangement is an `A` record for the root and a `CNAME` for `www`. Publish to whichever form you want as canonical; Surge [redirects the other](#www-and-the-root-domain) automatically.

## Checking the status

```sh
surge example.com status
```

(`surge example.com debug status` is the same command.) A custom domain moves through three states, and only the first is yours:

- **waiting on dns** — the domain doesn't resolve to Surge yet. The exact records to add are printed underneath.
- **securing** — DNS is right and Surge is provisioning the certificate. No action needed.
- **live** — verified by a real request against the edge, with the URL to visit.

Every publish reports the same status, so there's no need to run the check unless you want to watch it happen. DNS changes take time to propagate depending on the provider—Surge picks the domain up the moment the records are in place.

One more state applies to `surge.sh` subdomains published by a newly signed-up account:

- **ready** — published, and serving once you verify your email. A new account's `surge.sh` domains serve for their first 90 minutes; after that they show **ready** until the account's email address is verified. Click the link in the verification email (`surge verify` sends a fresh one) and they serve again—nothing to republish.

## Remembering the domain

Publish to the domain once and Surge records it in a [`CNAME` file](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#the-cname-file) in your project—from then on, `surge publish` needs no arguments.

## Subdomains

Each subdomain is its own independent project—own revisions, own settings, own owner:

```sh
surge ./www  example.com
surge ./docs docs.example.com
surge ./app  app.example.com
```

On a delegated domain every subdomain already resolves to Surge; nothing to add. With a `CNAME` or `A` record at your own provider, each subdomain you publish to needs its own record—or a wildcard (`*`) record pointing at Surge covers them all.

## www and the root domain

You don't need to publish to both. Surge redirects the `www` form of your domain to the root automatically—or vice versa, if you publish to the `www` form. Either way there's exactly one canonical URL for every page, which is what search engines want to see. The redirect needs both hostnames to reach Surge: automatic on a delegated domain, and one record each with a `CNAME` or `A`. See [Clean URLs](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/clean-urls).

## HTTPS for your domain

Once the domain resolves to Surge, a free managed certificate is provisioned automatically and renewed before it expires—`surge example.com status` shows it happening. See [SSL & HTTPS](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl).

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl

# SSL & HTTPS

## surge.sh subdomains

Every project on a `surge.sh` subdomain is served over HTTPS automatically, covered by Surge's certificate. There is nothing to configure. A new `<name>.surge.sh` domain also [forces HTTPS](#forcing-https) from its first publish.

## Custom domains

Custom domains get free managed certificates, provisioned automatically. Once your [domain points at Surge](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains), the platform obtains a certificate from a trusted CA, installs it across every edge node, and **renews it before expiry**—no command to run. While that's happening the domain reports **securing**; when every edge is serving it, **live**:

```sh
surge example.com status
```

Delegated domains get a single wildcard certificate covering the root and every subdomain, so new subdomains are secured the moment they're published.

Inspect the certificate any time with `surge example.com debug certs`, check it node by node with `surge example.com debug audit`, or provision it on demand with `surge example.com debug encrypt`. Details of the commands are in the [CLI SSL docs](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/ssl).

## Forcing HTTPS

Having a certificate makes your project available over HTTPS; forcing HTTPS also redirects every plain-HTTP request. Publish with `--force https`:

```sh
surge ./dist example.com --force https
```

From then on, `http://example.com/…` answers with a redirect to the `https://` URL. This is the right setting for almost every project—browsers and search engines both favor it. The choice sticks with the project across subsequent publishes—no need to pass the flag again.

The same setting is available without publishing, as [configuration](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config):

```sh
surge example.com config --force https   # set
surge example.com config --force http    # pin to plain HTTP instead
surge example.com config --force null    # clear: serve both
```

New `<name>.surge.sh` domains start out with `force` set to `https`; `--force http` undoes it. Domains that already existed keep serving both until you choose. To also have browsers insist on HTTPS, set an [`hsts`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config#the-settings) max-age.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/clean-urls

# Clean URLs

Clean URLs take real work on most servers—rewrite rules, framework configuration, boilerplate. On Surge they're automatic for every project:

- `/hello-world` serves `hello-world.html`
- `/foo/bar/` redirects to `/foo/bar` when the content is `foo/bar.html`
- `/foo/bar` redirects to `/foo/bar/` when the content is `foo/bar/index.html`
- `www.example.com` redirects to `example.com` (or vice versa—whichever form you publish to is canonical)
- `http://` can [redirect to `https://`](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl#forcing-https)

Build your project with plain `.html` files and link to the extensionless paths—Surge resolves them. Directory-style URLs (`/guide/` backed by `guide/index.html`) work equally well; pick the shape you like and the other resolves or redirects to it.

## Why the redirects matter

Serving the same page at multiple URLs—with and without a trailing slash, with and without `www`—splits your search ranking and your analytics across duplicates. Surge's redirects guarantee each page has exactly one canonical URL, and everything else points at it with a proper redirect. There's nothing to configure and no way to get it wrong.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/spa-routing

# Client-Side Routing

Single-page applications route in the browser: `/settings/profile` isn't a file, it's a state your JavaScript renders after loading. That breaks on ordinary static hosts—a visitor landing directly on a deep link gets a 404 before your app ever runs.

On Surge, the fix is a naming convention. Copy your app shell, `index.html`, to:

```txt
200.html
```

When a request doesn't match any file in your project, Surge serves `200.html` **with a `200 OK` status** and leaves the URL untouched. Your app boots, reads the path, and routes—deep links, refreshes, and shared URLs all just work. This is the behavior `pushState` routing expects, and it works with React Router, Vue Router, or any client-side router.

Copy rather than rename, after every build (builds clear the output directory): `/` keeps serving `index.html`, and every other unmatched path gets `200.html`. Renaming works too, since `/` falls through to `200.html` as well.

```sh
cp dist/index.html dist/200.html
surge ./dist publish
```

## Mixing static files and app routes

Real files always win. If your build also emits `/pricing.html` or a `/blog/` directory of static pages, those are served normally—only genuinely unmatched paths fall through to `200.html`. So you can pre-render what benefits from it and let the app handle the rest.

## 200 versus 404

Both files catch unmatched URLs; the difference is intent and status code:

- [`404.html`](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-404) — "that doesn't exist," served with a `404` status. Right for content-first projects.
- `200.html` — "the app will decide," served with a `200` status. Right for single-page apps.

If both are present, `200.html` takes over the unmatched routes. Have your router render its own not-found view for paths it doesn't recognize.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-404

# Custom 404 Pages

When a visitor requests a page that doesn't exist, Surge serves your project's `404.html` if it has one—styled like the rest of your project, saying what you want said—with a proper `404 Not Found` status.

Add the file to the root of the directory you publish:

```txt
my-project/
├── index.html
├── about.html
└── 404.html
```

Then deploy as usual. Every unmatched URL on the project now renders your page:

```sh
surge publish
```

A good 404 page is small, loads instantly, and offers a way forward—a link home, your navigation, or a search box. Since it's just a page in your project, it can use your project's CSS and assets like any other.

Many static generators can emit a `404.html` for you (Jekyll, Hugo, Astro, and others have it as a convention)—if yours does, it works on Surge with no extra configuration.

Building a single-page app? You likely want [`200.html`](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/spa-routing) instead, so unmatched URLs boot your app rather than dead-ending.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/redirects

# Redirects

Redirects live in a `ROUTER` file (no extension) at the root of the directory you publish. One rule per line: a status code, the pattern to match, and where to send it.

```txt
301   /contact   /about
```

`ROUTER` files are a Pro feature—publishing a project that contains one prompts you to upgrade right in the CLI if you haven't already. See [Plans](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/plans).

## Status codes

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `301` | Moved permanently. Browsers and search engines update to the new URL. |
| `302` | Found—a temporary redirect, the classic form. |
| `307` | Moved temporarily, and the request method is kept. The original URL stays canonical. |

Use `301` for content that has genuinely moved; `302` or `307` for temporary detours you expect to undo.

## Pattern routes

Named segments capture parts of the path and substitute into the destination:

```txt
301   /my-blog/:title   /articles/:title
```

Now `/my-blog/my-first-post` redirects to `/articles/my-first-post`. Segment names are yours to choose. This is the tool for migrating URL schemes wholesale—for example, moving off a WordPress-style structure:

```txt
301   /:year/:month/:day/:slug   /blog/:slug
```

## Query strings and trailing slashes

Rules match the path only. A request's query string rides along to the destination, so with `301 /contact /about`, a request for `/contact?ref=hn` lands on `/about?ref=hn`. A trailing slash is forgiven too: `/contact/` matches the `/contact` rule (an exact match elsewhere in the file still wins).

## External redirects

The destination can be a full URL on another host:

```txt
307   /blog   https://medium.com/surge-sh
```

## A complete ROUTER

```txt
301   /:year/:month/:day/:slug   /blog/:slug
301   /contact                   /about
307   /code                      https://github.com/sintaxi/surge
```

Rules are one per line and publish with the project like any other file—so your redirect table is versioned alongside your code, and [rolling back](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) a revision rolls back its redirects too. The `ROUTER` file itself is never served.

Note you don't need `ROUTER` rules for the redirects Surge already does automatically—trailing slashes, `www` folding, and HTTPS enforcement are covered in [Clean URLs](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/clean-urls) and [SSL](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl).

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth

# Password Protection & Protected Paths

Protection lives in an `AUTH` file (no extension) at the root of the directory you publish. Every line is a rule: a path pattern, then who's allowed. Rules ship with your files when you publish—no dashboard, no separate setup, and no login code in your project; the edge handles everything before your files are served.

```txt
/admin/*   jane@example.com
```

`AUTH` is a Pro feature—publishing a project that contains one prompts you to upgrade right in the CLI if you haven't already. See [Plans](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/plans). (To lock a whole domain to the people who can publish it on any plan, use [`--private`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config#private-domains) instead.)

## Who's allowed

A rule lists one or more principals after the path. There are two kinds:

| Principal | Who it matches | How they get in |
|-----------|----------------|-----------------|
| `jane@example.com` | Exactly that address | The sign-in page |
| `*@example.com` | Anyone at that domain | The sign-in page |
| `collaborators` | Everyone who can publish the domain: the members of the [org](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams) that owns it, and anyone [invited before orgs](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams#collaborators-from-before-orgs) | The sign-in page |
| `user:password` | Whoever knows the password | Browser password prompt, or `curl -u` |

Identity principals send visitors to Surge's sign-in page. A rule names email addresses; the page offers three ways to prove one—sign in with **Google**, with **GitHub**, or with a **Surge account**'s email and password. The rule doesn't care which: whichever a visitor uses, a verified email that matches lets them in, for 12 hours across the whole domain. The people you name don't need a Surge account—any Google or GitHub account works as-is (GitHub counts every verified address on the account; Surge accounts sign in once their email address is verified, and are asked for their code as part of the same sign-in if they keep [two-factor auth](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#mfa) on). Credential principals are classic HTTP basic auth.

## Rules

Write as many rules as you need, one per line. The first rule that matches the request path decides; blank lines and `#` comments are ignored.

```txt
# who can see what
/admin/*     collaborators
/drafts/*    *@example.com
/internal/*  jane@example.com sam@partner.co
```

A `/*` pattern covers the entire domain (a bare `*` means the same thing):

```txt
/*   collaborators
```

`collaborators` follows the org on its own: once someone [joins](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams), they can sign in without you republishing.

## Passwords

A credential principal puts a password on a path instead of (or as well as) an identity:

```txt
/*         viewer:letmein
/staging/* team:sekrit
```

The first line is whole-domain password protection—the classic use. The second protects just a section. Visitors get the browser's password prompt; scripts pass credentials the usual way:

```sh
curl -u viewer:letmein https://example.surge.sh/
```

The two kinds mix on one line, which is exactly what a protected path with automation wants—people sign in with Google, CI fetches with credentials:

```txt
/reports/*   collaborators ci-bot:s3cret
```

## Notes

- The `AUTH` file itself is never served—it's consumed by the platform, not published.
- Because `AUTH` ships with your files, protection is versioned: [rolling back](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) a revision rolls back its rules too, and removing the file on the next publish removes the protection.
- Sign-in lasts 12 hours per domain. Visiting `/__surge/logout` on your domain signs out, and the page a signed-in-but-not-allowed visitor sees offers the same switch—useful for changing accounts.
- Removing someone takes effect on their next sign-in: update the rule and publish, or remove them from the org; existing sessions expire within 12 hours.
- Serve protected projects over HTTPS (automatic on `surge.sh` subdomains, automatic certificates on [custom domains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl)) so nothing is exchanged in the clear.
- A malformed rule stops the publish with a line-by-line explanation that names the fix—`jane@example.com` on its own suggests `/* jane@example.com`. Your project is never published with a policy you didn't write.
- Legacy `AUTH` files—bare `user:password` lines with no path—keep working exactly as before, as shorthand for `/* user:password`.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cors

# Cross-Origin Resource Sharing

Browsers block cross-origin use of certain resources by default—web fonts referenced from another domain, `fetch()` requests, WebGL textures, some SVG uses. If a project on Surge hosts assets that your *other* domains need to load, enable CORS for it with a `CORS` file (no extension) in the root of the directory you publish.

This is the setup for using a Surge project as an asset host: fonts shared across your properties, an icon set, a data file your apps fetch.

## Allow any origin

Put a single `*` in the file:

```sh
echo '*' > CORS
surge publish
```

Every response now carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` permitting any origin to use the assets. Right choice for public assets—fonts, icons, open data.

## Allow specific origins only

List the origins, one per line, instead:

```txt
https://example.com
https://blog.example.com
```

Only those origins are permitted; requests from anywhere else still get the browser's default blocking.

## Notes

- The `CORS` file itself is never served.
- CORS is free on every plan. The same policy can also be set from the platform side, without a file, with [`surge <domain> config --cors`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config#the-settings).
- The policy applies project-wide. If only some assets should be shared, put them in their own project (a dedicated `assets.example.com`, say) and give that project the `CORS` file.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn

# The CDN & Edge Network

Surge runs its own CDN, purpose-built for static projects. Every edge node serves your project directly—content, certificate, redirects, and headers—and every node learns about a publish, a rollback, or a configuration change the moment it happens. That's why they behave the way they do everywhere else in these docs: instantly, and in every region at once.

## The network

<p id="js-cdn-live" hidden></p>

Ten regions, on three continents' worth of coverage—the same table every publish prints, [live on the network page](https://surge.sh/network):

| Node | Location |
|------|----------|
| `sfo` | US, San Francisco |
| `jfk` | US, New York |
| `yyz` | CA, Toronto |
| `lhr` | GB, London |
| `ams` | NL, Amsterdam |
| `fra` | DE, Frankfurt |
| `blr` | IN, Bangalore |
| `sgp` | SG, Singapore |
| `nrt` | JP, Tokyo |
| `syd` | AU, Sydney |

Every project—Free or Pro—serves from all of them.

## How routing works

Visitors reach the node nearest to them, and the routing happens at the DNS layer. When your domain is [delegated to Surge's name servers](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains), those name servers are geo-aware: a resolver in Berlin is answered with Frankfurt's address, one in Melbourne with Sydney's. `*.surge.sh` domains route the same way. Domains pointed at Surge with a plain `CNAME` record resolve through the same entry point and reach the network without geo-answers from your DNS provider—delegation is recommended for exactly this reason.

Once a request arrives, the node answers it—content, certificate, redirects, headers—from the region the visitor reached, not from a distant server.

## How publishing propagates

This is the property the whole platform is built around: **a publish propagates to every node while the publish runs.** Your files upload once; the network distributes them to each region; and each node confirms individually—that's the per-node table in the publish output, checking off in real time. When the command prints `Success!`, every node in the list is serving the new revision. There is no propagation delay to explain to a client, no "give it a few minutes."

Production moves atomically. Every publish creates an immutable [revision](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions), and production is a pointer at one of them—so `rollback`, `rollfore`, and `cutover` are pointer switches executed across the network in moments. Nothing re-uploads. The undo is as fast and as global as the publish was.

The same broadcast machinery applies to [configuration](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config): change a setting and every node picks it up immediately.

## Lucid Caching

Every asset is served with the same carefully-chosen caching strategy, applied automatically:

```http
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate
ETag: "9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08"
```

Read together, these headers tell the browser: *keep this file, but check with the server before using it again.* The check is an ETag validation—a tiny conditional request that returns `304 Not Modified` when the file hasn't changed, or the fresh file when it has. The result:

- The browser **never downloads the same bytes twice**—not even HTML.
- A visitor **never sees a stale file** after you publish.
- You **never rename files to bust caches** or fingerprint asset paths.

It's the most aggressive caching that never serves stale content—which is why there's no cache configuration on Surge at all.

## Gzip

All compressible content types—HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, SVG, text—are gzipped automatically at the edge. Binary formats that are already compressed (images, video, fonts) are passed through untouched. Nothing to configure, no build step.

## Watching the network work

The network is inspectable from the CLI, node by node. [`surge <domain> debug status`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics#status) confirms the domain is live against the actual edge—`live` means real requests are being answered with a valid certificate, not that a control panel thinks so. [`debug audit`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics#audit) asks every node which revision it's serving and the state of its certificate. [`stats load`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics) charts where in the world your traffic lands, per datacenter. And if you ever need to force the network's hand, [`debug bust`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/analytics#bust) purges every node's cache—though routine publishing never needs it: propagation and the ETag model keep every visitor current on their next request.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/platform/plans

# Plans

Surge has two plans, both account-level: **Free** and **Pro**. Every project and domain on your account is on your account's plan—there's nothing to choose per project.

## Free—actually free

The core of Surge costs nothing, without trial windows or project caps:

- Unlimited projects and domains, with publishing under [rate limits](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#publishing-limits) that apply to every plan
- [Custom domains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains)
- Managed [SSL certificates](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/ssl), provisioned automatically, and forced HTTPS
- The [CDN](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cdn), [clean URLs](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/clean-urls), [revisions](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions) (the last 100 per domain), and [teams](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/teams)
- [Cross-origin resource sharing](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/cors) (`CORS` file or `config --cors`)
- [Private domains](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/config#private-domains) (`--private`), served only to the people who can publish them

## What Pro adds

Pro unlocks exactly two features:

- [Password protection & protected paths](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/auth) (`AUTH` file)
- [Redirects](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/redirects) (`ROUTER` file)

Current pricing is listed by the CLI itself—`surge plan` shows each plan with its price and perks—and on the [pricing page](https://surge.sh/pricing). The bill is the plan price: no overage charges, ever.

## Upgrading

You don't have to decide in advance. Publish a project that uses a Pro feature—an `AUTH` file, say—and the CLI walks you through upgrading right in the publish, card entry included. Or manage it explicitly:

```sh
surge plan            # interactive picker in the terminal
surge plan --web      # checkout in the browser
surge plan --manage   # plan, card & invoices in the browser
```

Upgrade, downgrade, or cancel at any time; `surge plan --manage` opens a private billing portal with your invoices. See [Account & Plans](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account) for the commands in detail.
