Source: https://surge.sh/docs/api/

# Surge API

The Surge API is the HTTP interface that both the [CLI](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/) and the [SDK](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/) are built on. Anything the CLI can do—publish, roll back, manage DNS, read analytics—happens through these endpoints, so anything the CLI can do, your own tools can do too.

If you're working in JavaScript, use the [SDK](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/) rather than calling these endpoints directly; it handles authentication, upload streaming, and response parsing for you. This section documents the raw HTTP surface for everyone else.

## Base URL

```
https://surge.surge.sh
```

There is no path-based versioning. Clients identify themselves with a `version` header carrying their own release number.

## Conventions

**Authentication** is HTTP Basic on every authenticated endpoint. Normally the username is the literal string `token` and the password is your API token—see [Authentication](https://surge.sh/docs/api/authentication).

**Responses** are JSON. Most errors use this shape:

```json
{
  "messages": ["domain must be valid."],
  "details": { "domain": "must be valid." }
}
```

A few don't: rate limits answer `{ "message": "…" }`, a missing revision list answers `{ "error": "…" }`, and some refusals send an empty `{}` with the explanation in a `reason` header. Read `messages`, then `message`, then `error`, then the `reason` header.

**Domains are resource paths.** A project is addressed by its domain: `DELETE /example.surge.sh` tears down that project, `GET /example.surge.sh/list` lists its revisions.

**Long-running operations stream.** The deploy, certificate, and custom-SSL endpoints respond with newline-delimited JSON (`Accept: application/x-ndjson`): one JSON object per line, emitted as the work progresses. A line with `"type": "info"` signals success. See [Deploys](https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys).

## Common status codes

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `200` / `201` / `202` | Success. |
| `401` | Missing or invalid credentials. The JSON body explains why. |
| `403` | Authenticated, but not allowed—no permission for the domain, a token whose scope doesn't cover the request, a project over the size limits, or a password used on an account with two-factor auth (`details.mfa: "required"`). |
| `404` | No such project, revision, or account. |
| `405` | Operation not available for this domain (e.g. DNS management on a non-apex domain). |
| `409` | Conflict—for example, deleting an account that still has projects. |
| `422` | Invalid domain. |
| `429` | Rate limited. On publishes the `reason` header names the limit, and `retry-after` gives the seconds to wait—see [Deploys](https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys#failures). Account creation is also capped per network (50 an hour). |

## A quick tour

```sh
# Mint a token with your email and password
curl -X POST https://surge.surge.sh/token -u you@example.com:password

# List your projects
curl https://surge.surge.sh/list -u token:YOUR_TOKEN

# Deploy a tarball
tar czf - -C ./my-project . | curl -X PUT https://surge.surge.sh/my-project.surge.sh \
  -u token:YOUR_TOKEN \
  -H "Content-Type: application/gzip" \
  -H "Accept: application/x-ndjson" \
  --data-binary @-

# Take it down
curl -X DELETE https://surge.surge.sh/my-project.surge.sh -u token:YOUR_TOKEN
```

## In this section

- [Authentication](https://surge.sh/docs/api/authentication) — tokens, account creation, verification.
- [Deploys](https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys) — the upload format, deploy headers, limits, and the event stream.
- [Endpoint Reference](https://surge.sh/docs/api/reference) — every public endpoint.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/api/authentication

# Authentication

Every authenticated request to the Surge API uses **HTTP Basic auth**. There are two credential forms:

| Form | Username | Password | Used for |
|------|----------|----------|----------|
| Token | the literal string `token` | your API token | Everything, day to day |
| Email + password | your email address | your password | Minting tokens |

## Minting a token

`POST /token` with email + password credentials returns a long-lived token:

```sh
curl -X POST https://surge.surge.sh/token -u you@example.com:password
```

```json
{
  "email": "you@example.com",
  "token": "6b1a5b7d0f8e4c…",
  "id": "tok-1a2b3c4d",
  "msg": null,
  "scope": [],
  "created_at": "2026-10-25T18:22:10.000Z"
}
```

The response is `201`. Tokens are valid for three years. Use the token for all subsequent requests:

```sh
curl https://surge.surge.sh/account -u token:6b1a5b7d0f8e4c…
```

This is the same token that `surge login` stores in your `~/.netrc`, and that [`surge token`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account) prints—so for scripting against the API you can simply reuse the CLI's token.

An account with [two-factor auth](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#mfa) on can't mint a token with its password: every password-authenticated request answers `403` with `details: { "mfa": "required" }`. Sign in with `surge login --browser`, then mint more tokens with a token, as below.

## Labelled and scoped tokens

`POST /token` takes an optional JSON body, and works with token credentials as well as a password:

```sh
curl -X POST https://surge.surge.sh/token -u token:YOUR_TOKEN \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "msg": "ci", "scope": ["example.com"] }'
```

- `msg` labels the token (up to 140 characters).
- `scope` restricts it to the listed domains. A scoped token can publish to those domains and run their project calls (revisions, settings, analytics, teardown); account-wide routes and the domain's DNS, collaborators, plan, and certificate changes answer `403`. Scoping to a domain the account can't publish to is refused with `403`.

The rest of the token lifecycle:

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `GET /tokens` | The account's tokens: `id`, `msg`, `scope`, `uses`, `created_at`, `last_used_at`. Never the secret. |
| `DELETE /tokens/:id` | Expire a token by its `tok-` id. `204`. |

## Account creation

There is no separate signup endpoint. Authenticating with an email address that has no account **creates the account** with that email and password. This is how the CLI's first `surge` run registers you, and it applies to `POST /token` as well: mint a token with fresh credentials and you've created an account. New accounts are capped per network—past 50 in an hour from one IP, creation answers `429` with `retry-after`.

## The account object

`GET /account` returns the authenticated account, including plan and card status:

```json
{
  "email": "you@example.com",
  "email_verified_at": "2026-05-01T18:22:10.000Z",
  "created_at": "2024-01-15T09:30:00.000Z",
  "plan": { "name": "Free" },
  "card": null
}
```

A `401` here means the token has expired or been removed—mint a new one.

## Email verification

`POST /verification` (authenticated) sends a verification link to the account's email address:

- `200` `{ "verified": true }` — already verified, nothing sent.
- `201` `{ "verified": false, "sent": true }` — verification email sent.
- `200` `{ "verified": false, "sent": false, "msg": "…" }` — an email was already sent within the last five minutes.

Verify early: unverified accounts publish under half the usual rate limits, and a newly signed-up account's `surge.sh` domains stop serving after their first 90 minutes—`GET /:domain/status` reports them as `ready`—until the email is verified.

## Password reset

`POST /token/reset/:email` (no authentication) sends password reset instructions:

```sh
curl -X POST https://surge.surge.sh/token/reset/you@example.com
```

Always responds `201`, whether or not the email matches an account.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys

# Deploys

A deploy is a single `PUT` to the project's domain, with the project packed as a gzipped tarball in the request body. The response is a live stream of newline-delimited JSON describing the publish as it happens: upload, propagation to the CDN, certificate work, and the final result.

```
PUT /:domain
```

## Request

```
PUT /my-project.surge.sh HTTP/1.1
Host: surge.surge.sh
Authorization: Basic dG9rZW46…
Content-Type: application/gzip
Accept: application/x-ndjson
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
version: 1.0.0
file-count: 42
project-size: 123456
```

The body is a **gzipped tar archive** of the project directory. Notes on the format the official clients produce:

- Entries are prefixed with a single top-level directory (the server unpacks with the first path segment stripped), so `project/index.html` becomes `/index.html`.
- Files matched by the default ignore rules (`.git`, dotfiles, `*.*~` backups, `node_modules`, `bower_components`) and by the project's `.surgeignore` are excluded before packing.
- A single `.html` file can be published by packing it alone as `index.html`.
- The official clients first ask `POST /:domain/carry` which files the live revision already has, and pack only the rest (the `carry-ticket` header ties the two requests together). It's an optimization; a full tarball always works.

### Deploy headers

Metadata about the deploy travels in request headers:

| Header | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `version` | Your client's version string. |
| `file-count` | Number of files in the archive—used for progress totals and limits. |
| `project-size` | Total bytes—used for progress and limits. |
| `message` | A deploy message, shown in the revision list (`surge <domain> revs`). |
| `stage` | Set to make this a preview deploy: uploaded and given a revision preview URL, but not cut over to production. |
| `add` / `rem` | Comma-separated emails. `rem` removes collaborators invited before orgs; `add` invites no one now and the `info` line says so. |
| `argv` | JSON of the client's parsed arguments. Domain settings ride here and are applied on publish—`{ "force": "https" }`, `{ "private": true }`—the same keys as [`PUT /:domain/settings`](https://surge.sh/docs/api/reference#settings-analytics). |

## The response stream

The server responds `200` and begins streaming JSON objects, one per line. Each object has a `type`. In a typical successful deploy you'll see, in order:

```json
{ "type": "progress", "id": "upload", "written": 51200, "total": 123456 }
{ "type": "progress", "id": "cdn", "written": 12, "total": 42, "file": "index.html" }
{ "type": "cert", "data": { "issuer": "Let's Encrypt", "altnames": ["my-project.surge.sh"], "expiresInWords": "89 days" } }
{ "type": "subscription", "data": null }
{ "type": "info", "urls": [...], "instances": [...], "metadata": {...}, "config": {...} }
```

| Type | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `progress` | Progress through a phase. `id` is `upload`, `cdn`, or `encrypt`; the final message of a phase carries `"end": true`. |
| `cert` | Certificate details, when certificate work happens during the deploy. |
| `subscription` | The project's plan, if any. |
| `collect` | Payment required—carries `plan`, `perks`, `stripe_pk`, and a `checkout_url`. The deploy will not complete until the account subscribes. |
| `msg` | A human-readable server message: `{ payload: { msg, status } }`. |
| `error` | The deploy was refused mid-stream: `{ error: { message } }`—a project over the size limits, an `AUTH` file without Pro, a CDN failure. Nothing was published. |
| `info` | **The success marker.** Contains the deploy result: `urls` (where the project is reachable, including the revision preview URL), `instances` (the edge nodes serving it), `metadata` (revision id, message, file counts, sizes; `metadata.preview` is the preview host), and `cta` (one line the server wants shown, when it has one). |

A stream that ends without an `info` line means the deploy did not succeed. Note that a refusal can arrive *inside* a `200` stream as an `error` line—the status code alone doesn't mean success.

### Failures

Failures before the stream starts arrive as plain HTTP errors:

| Status | Reason |
|--------|--------|
| `401` | Invalid or expired token. The explanation is in the JSON body. |
| `403` | No permission to publish to this domain (the `reason` header says why when it can), a token scoped elsewhere, or a project whose declared `file-count`/`project-size` exceed the limits (10,100 files / 450 MB; `reason: Unable to publish. Application too large`). A project that only goes over during the upload is stopped with an in-stream `error` line instead. |
| `422` | The domain is invalid. |
| `429` | Rate limited. Per 15 minutes: 30 deploys per domain, 60 per account, 240 per IP. Per 24 hours: 200 per domain, 500 per account. Halved for unverified accounts. Body `{ "message": "…" }`. The `retry-after` header gives the seconds until the window allows another deploy; rejected attempts count toward the window, so wait it out rather than retrying. See [publishing limits](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#publishing-limits). |

## Revisions and previews

Every deploy creates a **revision**, identified by a millisecond timestamp, and each revision gets its own preview URL—`<rev>-example.surge.sh` for a `surge.sh` subdomain, `<rev>--example-com.surge.sh` for a custom domain. Surge keeps the last 100 revisions per domain. A normal deploy is cut over to production immediately; a deploy with the `stage` header stops after upload, leaving production untouched until you cut it over.

Revisions are managed with a small family of endpoints—list, rollback, rollfore, cutover, discard—documented in the [Endpoint Reference](https://surge.sh/docs/api/reference), and correspond directly to the [CLI's revision commands](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/revisions).

## Certificates over the same stream

Two more endpoints speak the same NDJSON protocol:

- `PUT /:domain/encrypt` — provision a managed SSL certificate for a custom domain. No body. Streams `progress` (id `encrypt`) and always ends with `info`, whose `certs` lists the domain's valid certificates—an empty list means none was issued.
- `PUT /:domain/ssl` — upload a custom PEM bundle (`Content-Type: application/x-pem-file`, raw body). Requires Pro. The response is always `200` and carries no `info` line; the outcome is the final `msg` line: `{ "type": "msg", "payload": { "msg": "the pem file has been applied", "status": "ok" } }`, or `"status": "error"` when the bundle is rejected.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/api/reference

# Endpoint Reference

All endpoints are relative to `https://surge.surge.sh` and require [token authentication](https://surge.sh/docs/api/authentication) unless noted. Errors mostly use the `{ messages, details }` shape described in the [overview](https://surge.sh/docs/api/). Calling from JavaScript? The [SDK Method Reference](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/reference) maps each endpoint to its method.

## Projects

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `PUT /:domain` | Deploy a gzipped tarball to the domain. Streaming—see [Deploys](https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys). |
| `DELETE /:domain` | Tear the project down. `200` `{ "msg": "project removed" }`. |
| `GET /list` | All projects on the account. Array of `{ domain, rev, timeAgoInWords, … }`. (`planName` is a legacy per-project label; read the plan from `GET /account`.) |
| `GET /:domain/metadata.json` | Metadata for the live revision: revision id, deploy message, publisher email, file counts, sizes, and the project's active config. `GET /:domain/:rev/metadata.json` targets a specific revision. |
| `GET /:domain/manifest.json` | The file manifest—a map of path to `{ size, md5 }`. Also available per revision. |
| `DELETE /:domain/cache` | Purge the project from every edge node's cache. `200` `{ "confirmed": [...], "unconfirmed": [...] }`. |
| `POST /:domain/carry` | Upload dedupe: send the project's file list and checksums, get back the files the live revision lacks and a `carry-ticket` for the deploy. Optional—see [Deploys](https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys#request). |
| `GET /:domain/status` | Where the domain stands: `{ status, action, https, reason, records }`. `status` is `waiting on dns`, `securing`, `ready` (a new account's `surge.sh` domain awaiting email verification), or `live`. |

## Revisions

Revision ids are millisecond timestamps (e.g. `1719852000000`). Each revision has its own preview URL, and the last 100 per domain are kept.

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `GET /:domain/list` | All revisions of the project: `{ rev, friendlySize, timeAgoInWords, publicFileCount, … }`. `404` if none. |
| `POST /:domain/rollback` | Point the domain at the previous revision. `201` `{ revision, former, instances }` when it moved, `200` when it was already there. |
| `POST /:domain/rollfore` | Point the domain at the next revision. Same responses. |
| `PUT /:domain/rev` | Cut over to the latest revision; `PUT /:domain/rev/:rev` to a specific one. |
| `DELETE /:domain/rev/:rev` | Discard a revision from the system. |

## Certificates

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `GET /:domain/certs` | Certificate information for the domain. |
| `PUT /:domain/encrypt` | Provision a managed certificate. Streaming NDJSON—see [Deploys](https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys#certificates-over-the-same-stream). |
| `PUT /:domain/ssl` | Upload a custom PEM bundle. `Content-Type: application/x-pem-file`. Pro only. Always `200`; the outcome is the final `msg` line's `status`. |

## DNS

DNS endpoints apply to **apex domains** delegated to Surge's name servers; on other domains they respond `405`. Records take the form `{ type, name, value, priority }`.

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `GET /:domain/dns` | The custom records you've added. |
| `POST /:domain/dns` | Add a record. `400` on validation failure. |
| `DELETE /:domain/dns/:id` | Remove a record. |
| `GET /:domain/zone` | The full zone, including the records Surge manages automatically. |
| `POST /:domain/zone` | Add a zone record. |
| `DELETE /:domain/zone/:id` | Remove a zone record. |

## Collaborators

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `POST /:domain/collaborators` | Closed: orgs share domains now. Answers `200` with each email `"status": "not sent"` and what to do instead; nothing is sent. |
| `DELETE /:domain/collaborators` | Revoke collaborators invited before orgs. Body `{ "emails": [...] }`. `202` `{ "successes": [...], "fails": [...] }`. |

## Settings & analytics

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `PUT /:domain/settings` | Update the domain's settings. Body is a map of setting → value—`force` (`http`/`https`), `redirect` (a domain), `cors` (a domain or `*`), `hsts` (seconds), `private` (`true`/`false`), any of them `null` to clear; the response echoes the resulting configuration. |
| `GET /:domain/analytics` | Aggregated traffic analytics for the past 14 days: visits, uniques, connections, bandwidth, status codes, encryption breakdown, sources, and per-file load. Cached for 15 minutes. |
| `GET /:domain/usage` | Bandwidth usage—same data source as analytics. |
| `GET /:domain/audit` | The project's state on every edge node, including a live TLS certificate check per node. |

## Account, tokens & billing

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `POST /token` | Mint an API token. Optional body `{ msg, scope }`. `201` `{ email, token, id, msg, scope, created_at }`. See [Authentication](https://surge.sh/docs/api/authentication#labelled-and-scoped-tokens). |
| `GET /tokens` | The account's tokens, by id. |
| `DELETE /tokens/:id` | Expire a token. `204`. |
| `PUT /tokens/:id` | Hand a token to an org the account is in: `{ org }`. Its value doesn't change. |
| `POST /token/reset/:email` | Send password reset instructions. No auth. Always `201`. |
| `POST /verification` | Send an email verification link. |
| `GET /account` | The account object, with plan and card. |
| `DELETE /account` | **Permanently delete the account.** `409` while projects still exist or the account is an org's only admin. |
| `GET /plans` | Available plans, the current plan, and card status. |
| `GET /subscription` | The account's current subscription. |
| `PUT /plan` | Subscribe to or change a plan. Body `{ plan, token, timestamp }`. |
| `PUT /card` | Update the payment card. Body `{ token }` (a Stripe source token). `201` on success. |
| `POST /upgrade/link` | Mint a browser checkout URL, valid 48 hours. `201` `{ url }`. |
| `POST /billing/link` | Mint a browser billing portal URL (card, invoices, cancellation), valid 48 hours. `201` `{ url }`. |

## Orgs

`:org` is an org's slug or id. Non-members get `404`, the same as for an org that doesn't exist. See [`surge orgs`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs).

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `GET /orgs` | The orgs the account belongs to, with its role in each. |
| `POST /orgs` | Create an org: `{ slug, name }`. The caller becomes its admin. Needs a verified email. |
| `GET /orgs/:org` | An org and its members. Members only. |
| `PUT /orgs/:org` | Change `slug` and/or `name`. Any member. |
| `DELETE /orgs/:org` | Remove the org. Admins only; refused while it holds domains (transfer or tear them down first). |
| `GET /orgs/:org/members` | Members and pending invites. A pending invite has no email: it's listed by `hint`, its code's first word. |
| `GET /orgs/:org/members/:email` | One member. |
| `POST /orgs/:org/invites` | Mint an invite: `201` `{ code, hint, role, expires_at }`. Nothing is emailed. Single-use, valid 7 days, up to 10 waiting per org. Optional `{ role }`: `member` (the default) or `admin`. Any member; inviting an admin, admins only. |
| `PUT /orgs/:org/members/:email` | Set `{ role }` to `admin` or `member`. Any change to or from admin is for admins. |
| `DELETE /orgs/:org/members/:email` | Remove a member. Any member; removing an admin, admins only; anyone, for themselves. |
| `POST /orgs/:org/join` | Join with `{ code }`, as the signed-in account. The same as `POST /claim` with an invite. |
| `GET /orgs/:org/tokens` | The org's tokens by id: scope, msg, `created_by`, uses, last used. Never the secret. Any member. |
| `POST /orgs/:org/tokens` | Add an org token: `{ msg, scope }`. `201` `{ org, token, id, msg, scope, created_by, created_at }`; the token is shown once. Any verified member, signed in as themselves; up to 10 per org. |
| `DELETE /orgs/:org/tokens/:id` | Expire an org token. `204`. Any member. |

An org token acts as the org. It publishes the org's domains (new ones become the org's), rolls back, cuts over, tears down, and reads `/list`, revisions, status and certs. Every other endpoint answers `403`. It outlives whoever added it.

## Transfers

A domain moves into an org you're in, out of one to your own account, or—by a transfer code—to anyone. Serving is unchanged. See [Moving a domain](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/orgs#moving-a-domain).

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `GET /:domain/owner` | Who owns the domain, for anyone who holds it: `{ owner: { account } }`, `{ owner: { org: { slug, name } } }`, or `"someone else"`. |
| `PUT /:domain/owner` | Move it: `{ to }` is an org slug you're a member of, or your own email. The owner account or any member of the owning org. Answers `{ domain, owner, from, collaborators }`. |
| `POST /:domain/owner/code` | Mint a transfer code: `201` `{ code, expires_at }`, valid 7 days. A new code cancels the last. |
| `POST /claim` | Claim with `{ code }`. A transfer code: the domain becomes the signed-in account's (`{ domain, owner, orgs }`), once, and only while the domain still has the owner it was minted under. An invite: the account joins the org (`{ org: { slug, name }, role, already }`). With `{ code, check: true }` it does nothing and describes the code instead: `{ check, kind: "transfer", domain, from, by, expires_at, yours }` or `{ check, kind: "invite", org, role, by, expires_at, member }`. After 10 codes that didn't work in an hour, per account or IP, answers `429`. |
| `POST /scrap` | Cancel `{ code }`: an invite, by any member of its org (`{ scrapped: "invite", org }`), or a transfer code, by whoever may mint one for the domain (`{ scrapped: "transfer", domain }`). |

Tokens scoped to a domain can read its owner but can't move it or mint a code.

## Sign-in sessions

These back `surge login --browser` and `surge mfa`; most tools never need them.

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `POST /login/session` | Start a browser sign-in. No auth. `{ uuid, url, code, poll, interval, expires_in }`. |
| `POST /login/session/:uuid/poll` | Poll it with `{ poll }`: `status` is `pending`, `approved` (with `email` and `token`, once), or `gone`. |
| `POST /mfa/session` | Open the two-factor setup page for the account. `{ url }`. |

## Feeds & platform stats

| Method & path | Description |
|---------------|-------------|
| `GET /stats` | Public, unauthenticated platform statistics—deploy counts, bytes published, project totals. CORS-enabled. |
| `GET /pulse` | Public server-sent event stream of completed publishes, anonymized. CORS-enabled. |
| `GET /activity` | Server-sent event stream of every change on the account's domains. Authenticated. |

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/

# Surge SDK

`surge-sdk` is the JavaScript library that the [Surge CLI](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/) is built on. If you're building a deployment tool, a static generator with a "publish" button, or your own CI tooling, the SDK gives you the same publishing machinery the official CLI uses—as a library.

It comes as two npm packages, versioned in lockstep:

| Package | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `surge-sdk` | JSON client for the Surge API—accounts, tokens, projects, revisions, DNS, plans, and analytics. |
| `surge-stream` | Streaming uploader that packs a directory into a gzipped tarball and publishes it, reporting progress as it goes. Also handles SSL certificate provisioning. |

You only need `surge-stream` if you want to publish or manage certificates. Everything else—listing projects, managing DNS records, rolling back revisions—works with `surge-sdk` alone.

## Installation

```sh
npm install surge-sdk surge-stream
```

## A first taste

```js
var surgeSDK    = require("surge-sdk")
var surgeStream = require("surge-stream")

var sdk = surgeSDK({ endpoint: "https://surge.surge.sh" }, surgeStream)

sdk.publish("./my-project", "my-project.surge.sh", { user: "token", pass: token })
  .on("progress", function(p){ process.stdout.write(".") })
  .on("success",  function(){ console.log("\nPublished!") })
  .on("fail",     function(){ console.error("\nDeploy failed") })
```

## How the pieces fit together

The SDK is a thin, stateless client for the [Surge API](https://surge.sh/docs/api/):

- **JSON methods** (`list`, `teardown`, `rollback`, `dns`, …) follow Node's callback convention: `sdk.method(args, creds, function(err, data){ … })`.
- **Streaming methods** (`publish`, `encrypt`, `ssl`) return an `EventEmitter` that relays live progress events from the server as the work happens.
- **Credentials are supplied on every call.** The SDK stores nothing on disk—token storage, prompting, and login flows are the caller's concern. (The CLI, for instance, keeps its token in `~/.netrc`.)

## Where to go next

- [Client & Authentication](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/client) — create a client and obtain a token.
- [Publishing & Streams](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/publishing) — deploy a directory and track progress events.
- [Method Reference](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/reference) — every method, with signatures and error shapes.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/client

# Client & Authentication

## Creating a client

`surge-sdk` exports a single factory function. Call it with a configuration object, and optionally the `surge-stream` module:

```js
var surgeSDK    = require("surge-sdk")
var surgeStream = require("surge-stream")

var sdk = surgeSDK({
  endpoint: "https://surge.surge.sh"
}, surgeStream)
```

### Configuration options

| Option | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `endpoint` | string, required | Base URL of the Surge API. Use `https://surge.surge.sh` for the public platform. |
| `defaults` | object, optional | Map of HTTP status code → handler function, called whenever a response with that status is received. See [status handlers](#status-handlers) below. |

The second argument, `surgeStream`, is the `surge-stream` module itself—not an instance. When you pass it, the SDK wires up the three streaming methods (`publish`, `encrypt`, `ssl`). If you omit it, those three methods become no-ops that log `` `surge-stream` not found ``, so pass it whenever you intend to deploy.

## Supplying credentials

The SDK is stateless: every method takes a credentials argument, and nothing is persisted between calls. Credentials can take any of these shapes:

```js
// A token (the usual case)
{ user: "token", pass: "6b1a5b7d…" }

// A bare token string is shorthand for the same thing
"6b1a5b7d…"

// Email and password (only needed to mint a token)
{ user: "you@example.com", pass: "your-password" }
```

Under the hood, credentials are sent as HTTP Basic auth. `username`/`password` keys work as aliases for `user`/`pass`.

## Getting a token

Exchange an email and password for a long-lived token with `sdk.token(creds, [args], callback)`. This is the only call that needs a password—everything after it uses the token:

```js
sdk.token({ user: "you@example.com", pass: password }, function(err, creds){
  if (err) return console.error(err)   // err.status === 401 → bad credentials

  // creds is ready to pass to any other method:
  // { user: "token", pass: "6b1a5b7d…" }

  sdk.account(creds, function(err, account){
    console.log("Logged in as " + account.email)
  })
})
```

Signing in with an email address that has no account yet **creates the account**—the same behavior as `surge login` in the CLI. There is no separate registration call. (New accounts are capped per network: past 50 in an hour from one IP, creation answers `429`.)

Two cases refuse a password:

- **Two-factor auth.** An account with [two-factor auth](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#mfa) on can't mint a token with its password—every password-authenticated call answers `403` with `details: { mfa: "required" }`. Tokens for those accounts come from the browser sign-in (`surge login --browser`) or `surge tokens add`.
- **Bad credentials.** `401`, with the reason in the JSON body.

### Labelled and scoped tokens

`sdk.tokenAdd(args, creds, callback)` mints a token from an existing token or password, with a label and an optional scope—the same call as [`surge tokens add`](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/account#tokens):

```js
sdk.tokenAdd({ msg: "ci", scope: ["example.com"] }, creds, function(err, record){
  // record: { email, token, id, msg, scope, created_at }
  console.log(record.id + " " + record.token)   // tok-1a2b3c4d 6b1a5b7d…
})
```

A scoped token can publish to its domains and run their project calls, and nothing account-wide. `sdk.tokens(creds, cb)` lists the account's tokens (by id—never the secret), and `sdk.tokenRem(id, creds, cb)` expires one.

Where you store the token is up to your application. The Surge CLI writes it to the user's `~/.netrc` file (keyed by API host, with `0600` permissions), which is a good convention for command line tools. For CI and server environments, an environment variable is typical.

To send a password reset email, use `sdk.reset(email, callback)`—no authentication required.

## Verifying the account

`sdk.account(creds, callback)` returns the account object:

```json
{
  "email": "you@example.com",
  "email_verified_at": "2026-05-01T18:22:10.000Z",
  "role": 4,
  "plan": { "name": "Free" },
  "card": null
}
```

Use it at startup to validate a stored token: a `401` means the token has expired or been removed (`surge tokens rem`), and you should re-run the token flow.

## Status handlers

The `defaults` option lets you register cross-cutting handlers for specific HTTP status codes—useful for handling authorization failures in one place instead of in every callback:

```js
var sdk = surgeSDK({
  endpoint: "https://surge.surge.sh",
  defaults: {
    403: function(err, response, body){
      console.error("Unauthorized.")
      process.exit(1)
    }
  }
})
```

Handlers receive `(error, response, body)` and run before the method's own callback. The SDK itself never writes to stdout, and errors always reach the callback whether or not a handler is registered.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/publishing

# Publishing & Streams

The streaming methods—`publish` and `encrypt`—each return a Node.js `EventEmitter` rather than taking a callback. The Surge API responds to these operations with a live stream of newline-delimited JSON, and the SDK re-emits each message as an event, so your tool can show real progress while the work happens.

These methods are only available when the client was constructed with the `surge-stream` module—see [Client & Authentication](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/client).

## Publishing a project

```js
sdk.publish(projectPath, domain, creds, headers, argv)
```

| Argument | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `projectPath` | Directory to deploy—or a single `.html` file, published as the domain's `index.html`. Files are gathered recursively, filtered by Surge's default ignore rules plus a `.surgeignore` file if one exists, then packed into a gzipped tarball and streamed to the API. |
| `domain` | Target domain, e.g. `"my-project.surge.sh"`. |
| `creds` | Credentials—normally `{ user: "token", pass: token }`. |
| `headers` | Optional object of extra HTTP headers. This is how deploy metadata travels: `version` (your client's version), `message`, `stage`, and so on—see [deploy headers](https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys#deploy-headers). `file-count` and `project-size` are filled in from the project when you leave them out. |
| `argv` | Optional parsed-arguments object; serialized into an `argv` header for the server. |

A complete example, modelled on how the CLI itself deploys:

```js
sdk.publish("./my-project", "my-project.surge.sh",
  { user: "token", pass: token },
  {
    "version":   "1.0.0",           // your tool's version
    "timestamp": new Date().toJSON()
  }
)
.on("progress", function(p){
  // p.id is the phase: "upload", "cdn", or "encrypt"
  // p.written / p.total track completion; p.file names the current file
})
.on("info", function(info){
  // The deploy result: info.urls, info.instances, info.metadata
})
.on("error",   function(e){ console.error(e.error ? e.error.message : e) })
.on("success", function(){ console.log("Published!") })
.on("fail",    function(){ console.error("Deploy failed") })
```

For projects over 1 MB, `publish` first asks which files the domain's live revision already has and uploads only the rest; a `carry` event reports `{ carried, sent }`. Nothing about the result differs.

## Stream events

Every JSON message from the server is emitted twice: once as a generic `data` event with the full object, and once as an event named after the message's `type` field (`progress`, `info`, `users`, `cert`, `subscription`, `collect`, `msg`, `error`). The message types and their payloads are the wire protocol, documented once in [Deploys: the response stream](https://surge.sh/docs/api/deploys#the-response-stream).

On top of those, the client emits lifecycle events of its own:

| Event | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `success` | The stream ended after an `info` message was received. The deploy is live. |
| `fail` | The stream ended without an `info` message, or the request failed outright. |
| `error` | The deploy was refused mid-stream—the server's `{ error: { message } }` line (project too large, an `AUTH` file without Pro, a CDN failure), a single file the SDK can't publish, or a transport error. Always attach a listener: an unhandled `error` event throws. |
| `unauthorized` | HTTP 401—the token is invalid or expired. |
| `forbidden` | HTTP 403—authenticated but not permitted (no access to the domain, token scope, project too large). Payload is the `reason` header when the server sends one. |
| `invalid` | HTTP 422—the domain is invalid. |
| `ratelimited` | HTTP 429—too many publishes in the window ([limits](https://surge.sh/docs/cli/publishing#publishing-limits)). Payload is the reason string, including when to retry. |
| `response` | The raw HTTP response, before any body—status code and headers. |
| `single` | A single file is being published: `{ file, as, local }`, where `local` lists files the page references that stay behind. |
| `skipped` | Paths left out because they have no content (dangling or looping symlinks, sockets). |
| `carry` | Upload dedupe: `{ carried, sent }`. |

Treat `success`/`fail` as the authoritative outcome; `info` merely carries the result payload.

## Provisioning a certificate

`encrypt` asks the platform to provision a free SSL certificate for a custom domain. Same event model, no request body:

```js
sdk.encrypt("example.com", { user: "token", pass: token }, { version: "1.0.0" })
  .on("info",    function(info){ console.log(info.certs.length + " valid certificate(s)") })
  .on("success", function(){ console.log("Request finished") })
```

The stream always ends with an `info` line, so `success` means the request ran—not that a certificate was issued. Read `info.certs` (the domain's valid certificates once the attempt is done), or ask afterwards with `sdk.certs()` or `sdk.status()`.

---

Source: https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/reference

# Method Reference

Every JSON method follows Node's callback convention—the last argument is always `function(err, data)`. Arguments marked *optional* (in brackets) may be omitted entirely; the remaining arguments shift left. `creds` is a credentials object as described in [Client & Authentication](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/client).

The streaming methods (`publish`, `encrypt`, `ssl`) return an `EventEmitter` instead and are covered in [Publishing & Streams](https://surge.sh/docs/sdk/publishing). Request and response bodies for each endpoint are in the [API Endpoint Reference](https://surge.sh/docs/api/reference); this page maps methods to them.

## Account & tokens

| Method | Calls | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| `token(creds, [args], cb)` | `POST /token` | Exchange email + password (or a token) for a token. Yields `{ user: "token", pass: "…" }`, ready to use as `creds`. `args` takes `{ msg, scope }`. |
| `tokenAdd([args], creds, cb)` | `POST /token` | Mint a labelled, optionally scoped token: `{ msg, scope: [domains] }`. Yields the full record `{ email, token, id, msg, scope, created_at }`. |
| `tokens(creds, cb)` | `GET /tokens` | The account's tokens by id: scope, msg, uses, created and last-used times. Never the secret. |
| `tokenRem(id, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /tokens/:id` | Expire a token by its `tok-` id. |
| `tokenTransfer(id, org, creds, cb)` | `PUT /tokens/:id` | Hand a token to an org you're in, its value unchanged. |
| `reset(email, cb)` | `POST /token/reset/:email` | Send a password reset email. No auth required. |
| `account(creds, cb)` | `GET /account` | Fetch the account: email, verification state, plan, card. |
| `verification(creds, cb)` | `POST /verification` | Send an email verification link. Yields `{ verified: true }` if already verified, `{ sent: true }` if sent, or `{ sent: false, msg }` inside the five-minute resend window. |
| `loginSession(host, cb)` | `POST /login/session` | Start a browser sign-in. Yields `{ uuid, url, code, poll, interval, expires_in }`. No auth. |
| `loginPoll(uuid, poll, cb)` | `POST /login/session/:uuid/poll` | Poll a browser sign-in: `status` is `pending`, `approved` (with `email` and `token`, once), or `gone`. |
| `mfaSession(creds, cb)` | `POST /mfa/session` | Open the browser page that sets up or manages two-factor auth. Yields its `url`. |
| `nuke(creds, cb)` | `DELETE /account` | **Permanently delete the account.** Fails with a 409 while projects still exist or the account is an org's only admin. |
| `stats(cb)` | `GET /stats` | Public platform statistics. No auth required. |

## Orgs

| Method | Calls | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| `orgs(creds, cb)` | `GET /orgs` | Every org the account belongs to, with its role. |
| `org(org, creds, cb)` | `GET /orgs/:org` | One org and its members. |
| `orgCreate({ slug, name }, creds, cb)` | `POST /orgs` | Create an org; the caller becomes its admin. |
| `orgRename(org, { slug, name }, creds, cb)` | `PUT /orgs/:org` | Change the slug, name, or both. Any member. |
| `orgRemove(org, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /orgs/:org` | Remove the org. Refused while it holds domains. |
| `orgMembers(org, creds, cb)` | `GET /orgs/:org/members` | Members and pending invites (`pending: true`, listed by `hint`). |
| `orgMember(org, email, creds, cb)` | `GET /orgs/:org/members/:email` | One member. |
| `orgInvite(org, [role], creds, cb)` | `POST /orgs/:org/invites` | Mint a one-time invite code, `{ code, hint, role, expires_at }`, to send yourself. `role` is `"member"` (the default) or `"admin"`. Any member; inviting an admin, admins only. |
| `orgRole(org, email, role, creds, cb)` | `PUT /orgs/:org/members/:email` | Set `role` to `"admin"` or `"member"`. Any change to or from admin is for admins. |
| `orgRevoke(org, email, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /orgs/:org/members/:email` | Remove a member (anyone may remove themselves). |
| `orgJoin(org, code, creds, cb)` | `POST /orgs/:org/join` | Join with an invite's code, as the signed-in account. |
| `orgTokens(org, creds, cb)` | `GET /orgs/:org/tokens` | The org's tokens by id, with who added each. Never the secret. |
| `orgTokenAdd(org, { msg, scope }, creds, cb)` | `POST /orgs/:org/tokens` | Add a token that acts as the org; the secret comes back once. |
| `orgTokenRem(org, id, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /orgs/:org/tokens/:id` | Expire an org token. |

## Transfers

| Method | Calls | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| `owner(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/owner` | Who owns the domain: `{ owner: { account } }`, `{ owner: { org: { slug, name } } }`, or `"someone else"`. |
| `transfer(domain, to, creds, cb)` | `PUT /:domain/owner` | Move the domain into an org you're in (`to` is its slug), or to your own account (`to` is your email). |
| `transferCode(domain, creds, cb)` | `POST /:domain/owner/code` | A code whoever claims takes the domain with: `{ code, expires_at }`. A new one cancels the last. |
| `claim(code, [{ check }], creds, cb)` | `POST /claim` | Any code: join the org an invite is for, or take the domain a transfer code names into the signed-in account. `{ check: true }` describes what the code would do and does nothing. |
| `scrap(code, creds, cb)` | `POST /scrap` | Cancel an invite or transfer code. |

## Projects & revisions

| Method | Calls | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| `list(creds, cb)` | `GET /list` | All projects on the account. |
| `list(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/list` | The project's revisions (the last 100). |
| `teardown(domain, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /:domain` | Take the project down and remove it. |
| `rollback(domain, creds, cb)` | `POST /:domain/rollback` | Point the domain at the previous revision. |
| `rollfore(domain, creds, cb)` | `POST /:domain/rollfore` | Point the domain at the next revision. |
| `cutover(domain, [rev], creds, cb)` | `PUT /:domain/rev/:rev` | Promote a revision to live (`PUT /:domain/rev`, the latest, when `rev` is omitted). |
| `discard(domain, rev, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /:domain/rev/:rev` | Delete a revision from the system. |
| `bust(domain, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /:domain/cache` | Purge the project from every edge node's cache. |
| `metadata(domain, [rev], creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/metadata.json` | Deploy metadata for the live revision, or `GET /:domain/:rev/metadata.json` for a given one. |
| `manifest(domain, [rev], creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/manifest.json` | File manifest—a map of path → size and checksum. `GET /:domain/:rev/manifest.json` with a rev. |

## Domains, DNS & certificates

| Method | Calls | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| `status(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/status` | Where the domain stands: `{ status, action, https, reason, records }`, with `status` one of `waiting on dns`, `securing`, `ready`, or `live`. |
| `certs(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/certs` | Certificate information for the domain. |
| `dns(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/dns` | List the domain's DNS records. |
| `dnsAdd(domain, record, creds, cb)` | `POST /:domain/dns` | Add a DNS record, e.g. `{ type: "MX", name: "@", priority: "10", value: "mail.example.com" }`. |
| `dnsRem(domain, id, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /:domain/dns/:id` | Remove a DNS record by id. |
| `zone(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/zone` | The full zone, including records Surge manages for you. |
| `zoneAdd(domain, record, creds, cb)` | `POST /:domain/zone` | Add a zone record. |
| `zoneRem(domain, id, creds, cb)` | `DELETE /:domain/zone/:id` | Remove a zone record by id. |

DNS methods only apply to apex domains you've pointed at Surge's name servers—see [Custom Domains](https://surge.sh/docs/platform/custom-domains).

## Collaborators

| Method | Calls | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| `invite(domain, { emails }, creds, cb)` | `POST /:domain/collaborators` | Closed: every email comes back `"not sent"`. Orgs share domains now. |
| `revoke([domain, ...emails], creds, cb)` | `DELETE /:domain/collaborators` | Revoke collaborators invited before orgs. Takes a single array mixing the domain and the emails to take off. |

## Settings & analytics

| Method | Calls | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| `settings(domain, props, creds, cb)` | `PUT /:domain/settings` | Update the domain's settings: `force`, `redirect`, `cors`, `hsts`, `private`. |
| `analytics(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/analytics` | Traffic analytics for the past 14 days. |
| `usage(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/usage` | Bandwidth usage data. |
| `audit(domain, creds, cb)` | `GET /:domain/audit` | Per-edge-node state of the project, including live certificate checks. |

## Billing & plans

| Method | Calls | Description |
|--------|-------|-------------|
| `plans(headers, creds, cb)` | `GET /plans` | Available plans, the current plan, and card status. |
| `plan(args, creds, cb)` | `PUT /plan` | Subscribe to or change a plan: `{ plan, token, timestamp }`. |
| `subscription(creds, cb)` | `GET /subscription` | The account's current subscription. |
| `card({ token }, creds, cb)` | `PUT /card` | Update the payment card with a Stripe source token. |
| `upgradeLink([plan], creds, cb)` | `POST /upgrade/link` | Mint a browser checkout URL (valid 48 hours). |
| `billingLink(creds, cb)` | `POST /billing/link` | Mint a browser billing portal URL (valid 48 hours). |

## Error handling

On success, callbacks receive `(null, data)` where `data` is the parsed response body. On failure, the error arrives as the **first and only** argument. Its shape depends on the endpoint:

```js
// The common shape — the response body, with status attached
{ messages: ["domain must be valid."], details: { domain: "must be valid." }, status: 422 }

// Some endpoints use a single message (rate limits among them)
{ message: "Rate limited. (domain). Try again in 9 hours.", status: 429 }

// A failure with no JSON body — described from the status
{ messages: ["request failed (502)"], details: { request: "request failed (502)" }, status: 502 }

// A network failure — the request never completed (no status)
{ messages: ["request did not complete"], errors: ["request did not complete"], details: { request: "did not complete" } }
```

Check `err.status` for the HTTP code, and fall back through `err.messages`, `err.message`, and `err.errors` when displaying the failure—the CLI does exactly this.
